domain.title: Networking & Interconnect
domain.why: When a huge AI model is trained across thousands of computers at once, the thing that usually breaks first isn't the math — it's the network connecting all those computers. Most computer science courses barely go past 'here's how one computer talks to another,' so engineers who can actually reason about network speed and bottlenecks between machines are rare and extremely useful. This domain builds that up from first principles.

sections.note: Layering is a filing system for protocols, not a description of how packets move. Learn what it explains before you learn where it lies.

concepts.t: The layer model, and where it lies

L0.body:
The stack as actually deployed, with the OSI number nobody uses in practice:

  L7  application   HTTP, DNS, gRPC          bytes with meaning
  L4  transport     TCP, UDP, QUIC*          port numbers, maybe reliability
  L3  network       IP                       global address, best effort, no order
  L2  link          Ethernet, 802.11         one hop, local address (MAC)
  L1  physical      copper, fibre, radio     symbols

  * QUIC is L4 semantics carried inside L4 UDP inside L3. The model has no box for that.
L0.cloze:
L4 is the {{c1::transport}} layer: TCP, UDP, QUIC.
L3 is {{c2::IP}}: global address, best effort, no ordering guarantee.
L2 is one {{c3::hop}}, addressed by MAC.
QUIC breaks the model because it implements transport semantics {{c4::inside UDP}}, at L4 over L4.
OSI layers {{c5::5 and 6}} (session and presentation) have no deployed counterpart in TCP/IP.

concepts.L1: A filing system for protocols, ordered by what each one assumes the layer below already solved. IP assumes the link delivers one hop; TCP assumes IP delivers datagrams somewhere, unreliably and out of order.
concepts.L2: Layering describes dependency, not encapsulation order, and not implementation. The place it lies hardest is that L4 checksums cover L3 header fields, so TCP and IP are not actually separable, and every NAT box has to know both.
concepts.L3: The clean version says each layer only talks to its neighbours. Trace one real fact against that. The TCP checksum is computed over a pseudo-header containing the IP source and destination addresses (RFC 9293 section 3.1). So a NAT rewriting an IP address invalidates the TCP checksum, which means every NAT must parse and fix up L4 state it supposedly cannot see. That single violation is why NAT traversal is hard, why NAT boxes hold per-connection state, and why QUIC encrypts almost its entire header: after thirty years of middleboxes inspecting TCP, the only way to make a transport evolvable again was to hide it from L3 devices. Layering is a good index and a bad map.

L4.prompt_tpl: A protocol designer proposes carrying {proto} directly over IP as a new protocol number rather than over UDP. Give the strongest argument against, in terms of what deployed L3 and L4 devices do.
L4.answer: Middleboxes drop unknown IP protocol numbers. NATs, stateful firewalls and load balancers key on the 5-tuple, which they can only build for TCP (6) and UDP (17); anything else has no ports, so a NAT cannot demultiplex return traffic to the right internal host. UDP encapsulation is not elegance, it is the only way to traverse the deployed internet.
L4.explanation: This is exactly why QUIC rides on UDP despite being a complete transport. Protocol ossification is the practical constraint that overrides the layering model: the layer boundary you are allowed to use is the one middleboxes already understand.

L4.prompt_tpl: The TCP checksum is computed over a pseudo-header containing the IP {field}. Explain what this implies for a device that rewrites IP addresses, and name the two consequences for real deployments.

field: source address, destination address and protocol number

L4.answer: It implies L3 and L4 are not separable: rewriting an IP address invalidates the TCP checksum, so a NAT must recompute it, which means the NAT must parse the transport header. Consequences: NAT boxes hold per-connection L4 state (so connections die when that state is evicted), and transports cannot evolve because middleboxes reject headers they do not recognise.
L4.explanation: The pseudo-header was a deliberate 1981 choice to detect misdelivered datagrams. Its lasting side effect is that it welded the layers together and made every address-rewriting device a transport-aware device.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team claims their {kind} tool is 'purely L3' because it only reads IP headers, and therefore cannot be affected by transport changes. Identify the flaw.
L4.answer: Nothing useful is purely L3. To make a forwarding or policy decision it needs ports, which are L4; to survive fragmentation it needs to reassemble, which requires L4 knowledge of which fragment carries the header. Reading only IP headers means it cannot distinguish two flows between the same host pair, and non-initial fragments carry no ports at all.
L4.explanation: The IP header gives you a host pair and nothing else. Any per-connection decision is L4 by definition, which is why every 'L3' device in practice parses L4 and breaks when L4 changes.

concepts.t: MTU, fragmentation, and path MTU discovery

L0.body:
Ethernet payload MTU is 1500 bytes. Subtract headers to get the TCP payload:

  1500 - 20 (IPv4) - 20 (TCP, no options)          = 1460  MSS
  1500 - 40 (IPv6) - 20 (TCP)                      = 1440
  1500 - 20 - 20 - 8 (timestamps, padded to 12)    = 1448  typical Linux

Over a tunnel that adds 50 bytes (VXLAN) the path MTU is 1450, so MSS is 1410.

  IPv4 header: DF bit set -> router sends ICMP Type 3 Code 4
               "fragmentation needed", carrying the next-hop MTU.
L0.cloze:
Ethernet MTU is {{c1::1500}} bytes of payload.
IPv4 MSS on a 1500-byte path is 1500 - 20 - 20 = {{c2::1460}}.
IPv6 MSS is {{c3::1440}}, because the IPv6 header is 40 bytes.
When the DF bit is set and a packet is too big, the router returns ICMP type 3 code {{c4::4}}.
IPv6 routers never fragment; fragmentation is done only by the {{c5::source host}}.

concepts.L1: The MTU is the largest L2 payload a link will carry. The MSS is what is left for TCP data after the IP and TCP headers. Path MTU is the minimum MTU along the route, and it is discovered, not known.
concepts.L2: PMTUD depends on ICMP messages that many networks blackhole as a security measure. The failure mode is not slowness: the handshake succeeds because SYNs are small, then the first full-size data segment vanishes and the connection hangs. Small requests work, large ones do not.
concepts.L3: Trace the blackhole, because it is the canonical works-for-me bug. Both ends complete the handshake with 60-byte packets over a path whose real MTU is 1450 because of a tunnel. Both advertise MSS 1460, derived from their own interface MTU, since neither can see the tunnel. The client then sends a 1500-byte segment with DF set. The tunnel ingress drops it and emits ICMP type 3 code 4, which a firewall discards. The client gets no signal, so it retransmits the same oversized segment on an exponentially backing-off timer, forever. Linux mitigates this with PLPMTUD (tcp_mtu_probing), which halves the probe on repeated timeouts instead of trusting ICMP.

L4.prompt_tpl: A path carries a {tunnel}-byte tunnel overhead over standard Ethernet. Compute the path MTU and the IPv4 TCP MSS that should be advertised, assuming a 20-byte IP header and a 20-byte TCP header with no options. Answer with the MSS to advertise.
L4.answer: path MTU = 1500 - tunnel; MSS = 1500 - tunnel - 40. For tunnel=50: 1450 and 1410. For 24: 1476 and 1436. For 8: 1492 and 1452. For 36: 1464 and 1424.
L4.explanation: MSS is always path MTU minus the IP header minus the TCP header. The 40-byte constant assumes IPv4 with no options; with TCP timestamps enabled Linux uses 12 more bytes, giving 1448 rather than 1460 on a clean 1500-byte path.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service works for {small}-byte responses and hangs for larger ones, always after the response headers are sent. The handshake succeeds. Name the fault, the exact signal that is missing, and two fixes.
L4.answer: A path MTU blackhole. The missing signal is ICMP type 3 code 4 (fragmentation needed), filtered by a firewall, so the sender never learns the path MTU and retransmits the same oversized segment forever. Fixes: clamp the advertised MSS at the tunnel ingress (TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu), or enable packetisation-layer PMTUD on the endpoints (net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1), which probes downward on repeated timeouts instead of trusting ICMP.
L4.explanation: The size threshold is the diagnosis. Headers fit in one small segment and arrive; the body needs full-size segments and does not. Blocking all ICMP is the usual root cause and it is a configuration error, not a hardening measure.

concepts.t: Ethernet, ARP, and the L2/L3 seam

L0.body:
Sending to 10.0.0.5 from 10.0.0.2/24 (same subnet):

  1. 10.0.0.5 is inside 10.0.0.0/24 -> it is on-link, no router involved.
  2. ARP cache miss. Broadcast to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:
       "who-has 10.0.0.5 tell 10.0.0.2"
  3. 10.0.0.5 replies with its MAC. Cache it (Linux: ~30 s to 60 s reachable).
  4. Frame: dst=that MAC, src=mine, ethertype 0x0800, payload = the IP packet.

Sending to 8.8.8.8 (off-link): ARP for the DEFAULT GATEWAY's IP, not for 8.8.8.8.
L0.cloze:
A host ARPs for the destination only when the destination is {{c1::on-link}} (inside its own subnet).
For an off-link destination it ARPs for the {{c2::default gateway}} instead.
ARP requests are sent to the broadcast MAC {{c3::ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff}}.
The ethertype for IPv4 is {{c4::0x0800}}; for ARP itself it is 0x0806.
IPv6 replaces ARP with {{c5::Neighbor Discovery}}, which uses ICMPv6 multicast rather than broadcast.

concepts.L1: ARP is the lookup from an IP address to the MAC address of the next hop on this link. It is the only place the subnet mask does real work: the mask decides whether the next hop is the destination itself or the gateway.
concepts.L2: A host never ARPs for an address outside its own subnet. Every packet to the wider internet is addressed at L2 to the gateway's MAC and at L3 to the final destination, so the L2 destination changes at every hop while the L3 destination never does.
concepts.L3: Watch the two addresses diverge; it is the most clarifying trace in networking. Host A (10.0.0.2/24, gateway 10.0.0.1) sends to 8.8.8.8. A computes 8.8.8.8 AND 255.255.255.0 = 8.8.8.0, not 10.0.0.0, so the destination is off-link. A ARPs for 10.0.0.1, gets the router's MAC, and emits a frame with L2 dst = router MAC and L3 dst = 8.8.8.8. The router strips the frame, decrements TTL, looks up its own next hop, builds a new frame with a different L2 destination, and forwards. The IP destination is untouched for the whole path. A wrong mask breaks exactly this test: mask a /24 host as /16 and it ARPs for hosts it can never hear, failing with no ICMP at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: Host 10.0.0.2 with mask {mask} and gateway 10.0.0.1 sends to 10.0.5.9. State whether it ARPs, and for which IP address.
L4.answer: With 255.255.255.0 (/24), 10.0.5.9 is off-link (10.0.5.0 != 10.0.0.0), so it ARPs for the gateway 10.0.0.1. With 255.255.0.0 (/16) both are in 10.0.0.0/16, so it is on-link and it ARPs for 10.0.5.9 directly. With 255.255.248.0 (/21) the host is in 10.0.0.0/21 which spans 10.0.0.0-10.0.7.255, so 10.0.5.9 is on-link and it ARPs for 10.0.5.9.
L4.explanation: The mask is applied to both addresses and the network parts compared. Getting a /21 wrong is the classic operational fault: the host believes a remote address is on-link, ARPs into the void, and times out with no ICMP unreachable to explain it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Across a path with {hops} routers, state which of the L2 destination address and the L3 destination address change, how many times, and why the answer differs.
L4.answer: The L3 destination never changes: it is the endpoint identity and is what makes forwarding possible. The L2 destination changes once per hop, so with h routers there are h+1 distinct frames and h+1 distinct L2 destination addresses. L2 addresses have meaning only within one broadcast domain, so they must be rewritten every time the packet enters a new one.
L4.explanation: This is the operational content of the layer split: L3 addresses are global and stable, L2 addresses are local and per-hop. TTL exists to bound the number of these rewrites when routing loops form.

sections.note: Do the CIDR arithmetic by hand until it is boring. Every subnet outage is this arithmetic, done wrong at 3am.

L0.body:
A /22 worked by hand. 10.20.30.44/22:

  prefix 22 -> host bits = 32 - 22 = 10 -> block size 2^10 = 1024 addresses
  mask = 255.255.252.0        (third octet: 256 - 2^(24-22) = 256 - 4 = 252)
  third octet of address = 30; 30 - (30 mod 4) = 28
  network   = 10.20.28.0
  broadcast = 10.20.31.255    (28 + 4 - 1 = 31)
  usable    = 10.20.28.1 .. 10.20.31.254   -> 1022 hosts

  python3 -c 'import ipaddress as i; n=i.ip_network("10.20.30.44/22",strict=False); print(n, n[0], n[-1], n.num_addresses)'
  10.20.28.0/22 10.20.28.0 10.20.31.255 1024
L0.cloze:
A /22 has {{c1::10}} host bits, so {{c2::1024}} addresses and 1022 usable.
Its mask is {{c3::255.255.252.0}}.
10.20.30.44/22 lies in the network {{c4::10.20.28.0}}/22, whose broadcast is 10.20.31.255.
The number of usable hosts in a /n IPv4 subnet is $2^{32-n} - 2$; the two subtracted are the {{c5::network and broadcast}} addresses.

concepts.L1: A prefix length says how many leading bits are the network. Everything else follows arithmetically: $2^{32-n}$ addresses, $2^{32-n}-2$ usable, and a network address that is always a multiple of the block size.
concepts.L2: The network address is not whatever you wrote down; it is the address rounded down to a multiple of the block size. 10.20.30.0/22 and 10.20.30.44/22 both denote 10.20.28.0/22. Tools that accept the sloppy form silently normalise it, and two engineers then argue about non-overlapping ranges that do overlap.
concepts.L3: Derive the mask rather than memorising it. For a /22 the host part is $32-22=10$ bits, so the block spans $2^{10}=1024$ addresses. Because 1024 is $4 \times 256$, boundaries land every 4 in the third octet: 0, 4, 8, ..., 28, 32. The address 10.20.30.44 has third octet 30, and $30 - (30 \bmod 4) = 28$, so the network is 10.20.28.0 and the broadcast is one below the next boundary, 10.20.31.255. The same rule handles any prefix: for /26 the block is $2^{6}=64$, so 192.168.4.130 falls in 192.168.4.128/26, range .128 to .191. The two unusable addresses are the all-zeros network identifier and the all-ones broadcast, which is why a /31 has no usable hosts under classic rules.

L4.prompt_tpl: For {cidr}, give the network address, the broadcast address, and the number of usable host addresses.
L4.explanation: Round the relevant octet down to a multiple of the block size; do not assume the address you were handed is the network address. Verify with python3 -c 'import ipaddress; print(ipaddress.ip_network(CIDR, strict=False))'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive, from first principles, the number of /{sub} subnets contained in a single /{sup}, and the number of usable hosts in each. Answer with the number of subnets.
L4.answer: subnets = 2^(sub - sup) when sub > sup, else undefined; usable hosts each = 2^(32-sub) - 2. For sub=26, sup=22: 2^4 = 16 subnets of 62 hosts. sub=24, sup=20: 2^4 = 16 subnets of 254. sub=28, sup=24: 2^4 = 16 subnets of 14.
L4.explanation: Every extra bit of prefix halves the block and doubles the subnet count, so the counts are always powers of two. The minus two is per subnet, which is why splitting a /24 into sixteen /28s loses 32 addresses to network and broadcast identifiers rather than 2.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer allocates 10.20.28.0/22 to one team and {other} to another and states the ranges do not overlap. Evaluate.
L4.answer: All three overlap. 10.20.30.0/22 normalises to 10.20.28.0/22, the identical block. 10.20.31.0/24 is entirely inside 10.20.28.0-10.20.31.255. 10.20.24.0/21 spans 10.20.24.0-10.20.31.255 and therefore contains the /22. Overlap is decided by comparing normalised network addresses and block extents, never by comparing the written strings.
L4.explanation: The /22 written as 10.20.30.0/22 is the trap: it is a legal spelling of 10.20.28.0/22 and most tools accept it without complaint. Always normalise before comparing, and prefer allocation tooling that refuses non-normalised input.

concepts.t: Longest-prefix match and the forwarding table

L0.cloze:
Forwarding picks the matching route with the {{c1::longest}} prefix, regardless of table order.
10.20.29.5 against that table matches /8, /16 and /22; the winner is {{c2::10.20.28.0/22}}.
The default route 0.0.0.0/0 matches {{c3::every}} address and always loses to any other match.
More-specific routes are how BGP hijacks work: announcing a {{c4::/24}} beats a legitimate /16.

concepts.L1: Forwarding is a single decision: among all prefixes that contain the destination, take the one with the most bits, and send to its next hop. Order in the table is irrelevant; specificity alone decides.
concepts.L2: Longest-prefix match is why a default route never causes an outage on its own, and why a single more-specific announcement can steal traffic globally. BGP hijacking is not a protocol bug, it is longest-prefix match working exactly as specified with an announcement nobody authorised.
concepts.L3: The rule has one consequence people misapply and one they underrate. Misapplied: adding a route can never be made safe by putting it 'at the bottom' of the table, because there is no bottom; a /32 blackhole route inserted anywhere wins over everything. Underrated: prefix length is a global lever. In 2008 Pakistan Telecom announced 208.65.153.0/24 to blackhole YouTube domestically; YouTube's own announcement was the shorter 208.65.152.0/22. Every router that accepted the /24 preferred it, and YouTube went dark worldwide for about two hours. Nothing malfunctioned. This is why operators filter announcements longer than /24, and why RPKI exists: BGP has no notion of who is entitled to a prefix.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given routes 0.0.0.0/0 via A, 10.0.0.0/8 via B, 10.20.0.0/16 via C, 10.20.28.0/22 via D, 10.20.30.0/24 via E, state the next hop for {ip}.
L4.explanation: Compute which prefixes contain the address, then take the longest. 10.20.31.255 is the instructive one: it is inside the /22 but not the /24, so it takes D even though it is numerically higher than addresses that take E.

L4.prompt_tpl: An AS legitimately announces {legit}. An attacker announces {evil}. Predict the effect on global routing and name the two deployed defences.
L4.answer: Every router that accepts the more-specific announcement prefers it by longest-prefix match, so traffic for that /24 is drawn to the attacker globally, with no protocol violation anywhere. Defences: prefix-length and IRR-based filtering by transit providers (commonly rejecting anything longer than /24), and RPKI route origin validation, where a signed ROA binds a prefix and maximum length to an origin AS so invalid announcements can be dropped.
L4.explanation: This is the 2008 YouTube hijack in miniature. The lesson is that longest-prefix match provides no authorisation whatsoever; every defence is external to BGP and is about who is allowed to say a prefix, not about how routers choose.

L0.body:
Source NAT rewrites the 5-tuple and remembers the mapping.

  outbound   10.0.0.7:51514  -> 93.184.216.34:443
  on wire    203.0.113.9:40122 -> 93.184.216.34:443
  return     93.184.216.34:443 -> 203.0.113.9:40122
  restored   93.184.216.34:443 -> 10.0.0.7:51514

  Table entry: (203.0.113.9,40122) <-> (10.0.0.7,51514) + TTL

  Rewriting the IP address invalidates the TCP checksum, so the NAT
  recomputes it -- the NAT is a transport-layer device by necessity.
L0.cloze:
Source NAT rewrites the {{c1::source IP and source port}} on the way out and reverses it on the way in.
It must keep {{c2::per-connection state}}, so it is stateful and its table can be exhausted.
Because the TCP checksum covers the IP addresses via the pseudo-header, the NAT must also recompute the {{c3::checksum}}.
When the mapping expires while a connection is idle, the connection does not close: it {{c4::hangs}}, because neither endpoint is told.

concepts.L1: NAT multiplexes many private addresses onto few public ones by rewriting the source IP and port and recording the mapping. It converts an address-family shortage into a state-table problem.
concepts.L2: The real cost is not the rewrite, it is that NAT invents connection state where the protocol had none. TCP endpoints can survive an hour of silence; a NAT with a 300-second idle timer cannot, and the connection dies without either endpoint receiving a FIN or RST.
concepts.L3: The half-open hang is the failure worth knowing. A client opens a TCP connection to a database and idles ten minutes. The NAT evicts the mapping at five. Both ends still believe they are connected: idle TCP sends nothing and expects nothing. At minute ten the client sends a query; the NAT has no entry for the inbound 5-tuple, so the reply is dropped or met with RST. The client retransmits until its own timeout expires. Every fix is a keepalive shorter than the shortest NAT timeout on the path: TCP keepalives (Linux tcp_keepalive_time defaults to 7200 seconds, far too long, so applications set it near 60), or application pings. This is why idle connection pools misbehave across NATs.

L4.prompt_tpl: A connection pool holds idle TCP connections for {idle} minutes across a NAT with a 5-minute UDP/TCP idle timeout. Describe the exact failure the application sees and the correct fix.
L4.answer: The NAT silently drops the mapping at 5 minutes. Both endpoints still consider the connection ESTABLISHED because idle TCP sends nothing. The next query is sent, the NAT has no entry, the packet is dropped or RST, and the application blocks until its own read timeout, then sees a connection reset or timeout on a connection it believes is healthy. Fix: a keepalive shorter than the NAT timeout (TCP_KEEPIDLE near 60 s, or application pings), plus a pool max-idle shorter than the NAT timeout.
L4.explanation: Raising the application timeout does not help; it only makes the stall longer. The only durable fix is traffic on the connection frequently enough that the NAT mapping is refreshed.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two hosts behind separate NATs must establish a direct {proto} connection. Explain why the naive approach fails and describe the technique that makes it work.
L4.answer: Neither NAT has an inbound mapping, so an unsolicited packet from outside is dropped: both sides can only initiate, neither can receive. The technique is hole punching: both hosts send outbound to the peer's public 5-tuple (learned via a rendezvous server, typically STUN), which creates a mapping in each NAT; the first packets are dropped but each one opens the return path, so subsequent packets traverse. It fails against symmetric NATs, which allocate a different external port per destination, so the port learned via STUN does not match; those require a relay (TURN).
L4.explanation: Hole punching is why UDP is the default for peer-to-peer despite TCP being available: a UDP mapping is created by a single outbound packet, with no handshake state to confuse the NAT.

concepts.t: DNS: the resolution path and its caching layers

L0.body:
Resolving www.example.com, cold, from a stub resolver:

  stub -> recursive resolver (/etc/resolv.conf)
    resolver -> root         "who serves .com?"        -> NS for com.
    resolver -> .com TLD     "who serves example.com?" -> NS a.iana-servers.net
    resolver -> authoritative "A www.example.com?"     -> 93.184.216.34, TTL 3600

Caches, innermost first, each with its own expiry:
  app/library (JVM, http client) -> OS stub (systemd-resolved, nscd)
  -> recursive resolver -> negative cache (SOA MINIMUM, RFC 2308)
L0.cloze:
A cold recursive lookup costs {{c1::three}} queries above the stub: root, TLD, then authoritative.
Each record carries a {{c2::TTL}} that bounds how long a cache may keep it.
Negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached too, governed by the {{c3::SOA}} record's minimum field, per RFC 2308.
The dangerous cache is the one that {{c4::ignores TTL}}: JVM and browser caches keep records past expiry, so lowering a TTL before a cutover does not reach them.

concepts.L1: DNS is a delegated hierarchy resolved by iteration: the recursive resolver walks root to TLD to authoritative, and every answer carries a TTL that licenses caching. The stub asks one question; the resolver asks three.
concepts.L2: Lowering a TTL before a migration only works if you lower it more than one old-TTL in advance, because caches populated before the change still hold the old value for the old duration. Cutting a 24-hour TTL to 60 seconds an hour before a cutover changes nothing for anyone already cached.
concepts.L3: The TTL-lowering mistake follows directly from when caches sample. A cache that fetched the record at $t_{0}$ with TTL $T_{\text{old}}$ re-queries at $t_{0} + T_{\text{old}}$, not before. Publish a shorter TTL at $t_{1}$ and only caches re-querying after $t_{1}$ see it, so it is not universal until $t_{1} + T_{\text{old}}$. To have every cache on a 60-second TTL by cutover $t_{c}$, publish the reduction no later than $t_{c} - T_{\text{old}} - 60$ seconds. The second trap is the layer that ignores TTL entirely: older JVMs cached successful lookups forever (networkaddress.cache.ttl of -1), so Java services kept hitting a decommissioned IP for days after DNS was correct everywhere else.

L4.prompt_tpl: A record currently has TTL {old} seconds. You want every cache to be observing a 60-second TTL by the cutover. How long before the cutover must you publish the reduction, and why? Answer with the lead time in seconds.
L4.answer: At least old + 60 seconds before the cutover. For 86400: 86460 s (about 24 h). For 3600: 3660 s. For 300: 360 s. Reason: a cache that sampled the record just before you published still holds the old value for a full old-TTL, so it cannot pick up the new TTL until old seconds have elapsed; it then needs one more short TTL to be safely in the short-TTL regime.
L4.explanation: The common error is publishing the reduction one short-TTL before the cutover. Caches populated before the publish are unaffected by it, so the worst case is bounded by the old TTL, not the new one.

L4.prompt_tpl: After a migration, {frac} of traffic still reaches the old IP for days, while dig against the authoritative server and against the public resolver both return the new address. Explain the mechanism and how to confirm it.
L4.answer: A cache that ignores TTL. dig queries the resolver and the authoritative server, which are correct; it does not query the application's own in-process cache. Long-running JVM services with networkaddress.cache.ttl set to -1, and some HTTP client libraries that resolve once at pool construction, hold the old address until restarted. Confirm by checking the old IP's connections for a stable set of source hosts and long-lived connections, and by restarting one suspect client to see its traffic move.
L4.explanation: The diagnostic principle: dig tells you what the DNS system says, not what the application resolved. When those disagree, the cache is above the resolver, inside the process.

sections.note: TCP is a sliding-window protocol with a timer. Everything else is elaboration. Build it once (CS144) and you stop guessing.

concepts.t: The three-way handshake and its cost in RTTs

L0.body:
client                                  server
    | --- SYN  seq=x, MSS, wscale, SACK-ok --> |   0.5 RTT
    | <-- SYN-ACK seq=y ack=x+1 ------------- |   1.0 RTT
    | --- ACK  seq=x+1 ack=y+1 -------------- |   1.5 RTT   (data may ride here)
    | --- HTTP GET -------------------------- |
    | <-- 200 OK ---------------------------- |   2.0 RTT

Cost to first byte of response, by stack:
  TCP + HTTP            2 RTT
  TCP + TLS 1.3 + HTTP  3 RTT
  TCP + TLS 1.2 + HTTP  4 RTT
  QUIC (1-RTT) + HTTP   2 RTT      QUIC 0-RTT: 1 RTT
L0.cloze:
The handshake is SYN, {{c1::SYN-ACK}}, ACK: the connection is usable after {{c2::1}} RTT of exchange, and the first response byte arrives at {{c3::2}} RTTs.
Adding TLS 1.3 costs one more RTT, for {{c4::3}} total.
The options that must be negotiated in the SYN, because they cannot be added later, are MSS, {{c5::window scaling}} and SACK permission.

concepts.L1: Three segments establish sequence numbers in both directions and negotiate the options that cannot be changed afterwards. The client may send data with its final ACK, so the connection costs one RTT before useful data, two before a response.
concepts.L2: Window scaling is negotiated only in the SYN and SYN-ACK, and only takes effect if both sides send it. A middlebox that strips the option from one direction leaves the connection working but capped at a 64 KiB window, which looks like a mysterious throughput ceiling rather than a failure.
concepts.L3: Count the round trips for a real page load and the design pressure becomes obvious. Over a 75 ms transatlantic path, TCP plus TLS 1.3 plus HTTP is three RTTs, or 225 ms, before a single byte of HTML arrives, and none of it is bandwidth-limited. This is why connection reuse dominates every other web performance lever, why HTTP/2 multiplexes onto one connection, and why QUIC folds the transport and cryptographic handshakes into one flight. The corollary is that the handshake is also where an attacker gets leverage: the server must allocate state on SYN and hold it for the SYN-ACK retransmission schedule, which is the SYN flood, and the reason SYN cookies exist.

L4.prompt_tpl: Over a path with RTT {rtt} ms, compute the time to the first byte of the HTTP response for TCP+TLS1.3+HTTP, and the extra cost of TLS 1.2 instead. Ignore processing time. Answer with the time to first byte in milliseconds for TLS 1.3.
L4.answer: TCP+TLS1.3+HTTP = 3 RTT; TLS 1.2 adds one more RTT for 4. rtt=75: 225 ms, extra 75 ms (300 total). rtt=150: 450 ms, extra 150. rtt=20: 60 ms, extra 20. rtt=250: 750 ms, extra 250.
L4.explanation: Handshake cost is linear in RTT and independent of bandwidth, which is why long-haul page loads do not improve when you buy more capacity. The only fixes are fewer round trips (QUIC, TLS resumption) or a shorter path (edge termination).

L4.prompt_tpl: A transfer between two hosts on a {rtt} ms path plateaus at about 5 Mb/s regardless of the link capacity, and tcpdump shows no retransmissions. State the most likely cause and how to confirm it from the SYN.
L4.answer: Window scaling is not in effect, so the receive window is capped at 65535 bytes, limiting throughput to window/RTT = 65535*8/0.1 s = 5.24 Mb/s at 100 ms. Confirm by checking that the window scale option appears in both the SYN and the SYN-ACK; a middlebox that strips it from one direction disables scaling for the connection. No loss is the tell: this is a window limit, not a congestion limit.
L4.explanation: Throughput with no loss is window over RTT. If that number matches 64 KiB / RTT almost exactly, scaling is off. Window scale is negotiable only during the handshake, so it cannot be repaired on an established connection.

concepts.t: Sequence numbers and the byte-stream abstraction

L0.body:
TCP numbers BYTES, not segments. seq is the number of the first data byte.

  ISN chosen randomly (RFC 6528), say 1000
  send 1460 bytes:  seq=1001  ..1460 bytes..
  send 1460 bytes:  seq=2461
  peer ACKs:        ack=3921    "I have everything below 3921"

  ACK is cumulative: ack=3921 says nothing about bytes above 3921.
  SACK (RFC 2018) adds "and also I hold 5381-6840", which is how the
  sender learns about a single hole instead of assuming loss of all.

  32-bit space wraps after 4 GiB; PAWS (RFC 7323) uses timestamps to reject wrapped duplicates.
L0.cloze:
TCP sequence numbers count {{c1::bytes}}, not segments or packets.
The plain ACK field is {{c2::cumulative}}: it names the next byte expected, and says nothing about bytes received above it.
{{c3::SACK}} adds explicit ranges so the sender can retransmit only the hole.
The initial sequence number is {{c4::randomised}} (RFC 6528) to make off-path injection hard.
The 32-bit sequence space wraps after {{c5::4 GiB}}; PAWS uses timestamps to reject old wrapped segments.

concepts.L1: TCP presents a reliable ordered byte stream and numbers every byte. Segment boundaries are an artefact of the MSS and the sender's write pattern; they carry no meaning and are not preserved.
concepts.L2: Because the stream has no record boundaries, a single write of 100 bytes may arrive as two reads, and two writes may arrive as one. Every protocol on top of TCP must carry its own framing, and the bugs that come from assuming otherwise appear only under load, when segments coalesce.
concepts.L3: The cumulative ACK is the design decision with the most downstream consequences. With cumulative ACKs alone, a sender that loses one segment out of ten in flight sees ACKs stall at the hole and learns nothing about the nine that arrived. The original recovery was go-back-N in spirit: retransmit from the hole. SACK fixes this by letting the receiver report the blocks it holds, so the sender retransmits exactly the missing segment. That is why SACK is negotiated in the SYN, and why disabling it (net.ipv4.tcp_sack=0, still done as folklore hardening) turns a single loss on a large window into a multi-segment retransmission.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service reads with a single recv() of {size} bytes per message and works in test but corrupts messages in production under load. Name the fault and the fix.
L4.answer: It assumes TCP preserves message boundaries. TCP is a byte stream: one recv() may return a partial message or several concatenated messages, and Nagle plus the MSS make coalescing far more likely under load than in a low-rate test. The fix is explicit framing: a fixed-size length prefix, or a delimiter, with a read loop that accumulates into a buffer until a complete message is present and then consumes exactly that many bytes.
L4.explanation: The test passes because at low rates each write becomes one segment and one recv. Load changes the segment pattern, not the protocol. Any code path that treats a recv() return as a message is wrong even if it has never failed.

L4.prompt_tpl: A sender has {n} segments in flight and the {k}th is lost. Contrast what it learns from cumulative ACKs alone versus with SACK, and state what it retransmits in each case.
L4.answer: With cumulative ACKs only, the receiver keeps ACKing the byte before the hole, so the sender sees duplicate ACKs but cannot tell whether the later segments arrived; a conservative sender retransmits from the hole onwards, wasting the bandwidth of everything that did arrive. With SACK the receiver reports the blocks it holds above the hole, so the sender retransmits exactly the one lost segment and keeps the rest of the window accounted for.
L4.explanation: Duplicate ACKs carry one bit of information: something arrived out of order. SACK turns that into an exact map. This is why SACK matters most on high-BDP paths, where a window holds many segments and go-back-N is ruinous.

concepts.t: The sliding window and flow control

L0.body:
The receive window is the receiver's free buffer space, advertised in every ACK.

  sender's usable window = min(cwnd, rwnd) - bytes_in_flight

  rwnd  flow control     "do not overrun MY buffer"      -- receiver's limit
  cwnd  congestion ctl   "do not overrun THE NETWORK"    -- sender's estimate

  Header field is 16 bits -> 65535 max, so RFC 7323 window scaling
  multiplies it by 2^wscale (wscale <= 14, so up to ~1 GiB).

  rwnd = 0 -> sender stops and probes with a window probe (persist timer).
L0.cloze:
The receive window {{c1::rwnd}} is advertised by the receiver and protects the receiver's buffer; the congestion window {{c2::cwnd}} is the sender's own estimate and protects the network.
A sender may have at most $\min(\text{cwnd}, \text{rwnd})$ bytes {{c3::in flight}}.
The window field is only {{c4::16}} bits, so window scaling shifts it by up to $2^{14}$.
When the advertised window reaches zero the sender must send a {{c5::window probe}} rather than wait, or it can deadlock on a lost window update.

concepts.L1: Two independent limits govern how much unacknowledged data a sender may have outstanding: the receiver's advertised window and the sender's congestion window. The effective limit is the smaller of the two, minus what is already in flight.
concepts.L2: Blaming congestion control for a throughput problem is usually wrong. If the receive window is the binding constraint, no congestion algorithm helps: the receiver is not draining its buffer fast enough, or its buffer is too small. Check which of the two is smaller before changing anything.
concepts.L3: The zero-window deadlock explains why the persist timer exists. Receiver advertises rwnd=0; the sender stops. The receiver's application drains the buffer and the receiver sends a window update, which is a pure ACK carrying no data. Pure ACKs are not retransmitted, because retransmission is driven by unacknowledged data and there is none. If that update is lost, the sender waits forever for a window that has already opened, and the receiver waits forever for data. TCP breaks the symmetry by making the sender responsible: the persist timer fires and it sends a one-byte window probe, forcing a fresh advertisement. Whenever both sides could wait, exactly one gets a timer.

L4.prompt_tpl: A receiver advertises a window of {rwnd} bytes and the sender's cwnd is {cwnd} bytes on a {rtt} ms path with no loss. Compute the achievable throughput in Mb/s and name the binding constraint. Answer with the throughput in Mb/s.
L4.answer: throughput = 8*min(rwnd,cwnd)/RTT. rwnd=65535, cwnd=1048576, rtt=10 ms: min is 65535 -> 52.4 Mb/s, receiver-limited. rwnd=4194304, cwnd=131072, rtt=80 ms: min is 131072 -> 13.1 Mb/s, congestion-limited. rwnd=262144, cwnd=1048576, rtt=80 ms: min is 262144 -> 26.2 Mb/s, receiver-limited.
L4.explanation: Throughput on a lossless path is simply window over RTT. Identify which window is smaller before tuning: enlarging cwnd when rwnd binds changes nothing, and is the most common wasted congestion-control experiment.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a lost pure ACK carrying a window update can deadlock a TCP connection, and derive which endpoint must hold the recovery timer. Assume a window of {w} bytes just opened.
L4.answer: Pure ACKs consume no sequence space and so are never retransmitted; retransmission is triggered by unacknowledged data. If the window update is lost, the sender still believes rwnd=0 and sends nothing, while the receiver has no data to acknowledge and therefore sends nothing. Both wait. The timer must be held by the sender, because only the sender can generate the data that will elicit a fresh ACK carrying the current window: the receiver has no way to force the sender to speak. Hence the persist timer and the one-byte window probe.
L4.explanation: The general rule this instance teaches: in any two-party protocol where both sides can legitimately be silent, exactly one side must own a timer, and it must be the side that can generate traffic the other is obliged to answer.

prereqs: Sequence numbers and the byte-stream abstraction

L0.body:
BDP = bandwidth x round-trip time. It is the amount of data that must be
in flight to keep a pipe full.

  10 Gb/s x 100 ms  = 1e9 bits   = 125 MB   = 119 MiB
   1 Gb/s x 100 ms  = 1e8 bits   =  12.5 MB
  25 Gb/s x  70 ms  = 1.75e9 bit = 219 MB
 100 Gb/s x  50 us  = 5e6 bits   = 625 kB     (in-datacenter)
 400 Gb/s x   5 us  = 2e6 bits   = 250 kB     (training fabric)

Ceiling without window scaling: 65535 B / 0.1 s = 5.24 Mb/s.
Linux autotunes to net.ipv4.tcp_rmem[2] (this host: 33554432 = 32 MiB).
L0.cloze:
BDP is bandwidth multiplied by {{c1::round-trip time}}, and equals the bytes that must be unacknowledged to keep the link busy.
$10$ Gb/s over a $100$ ms RTT gives a BDP of {{c2::125}} MB.
If the window is smaller than the BDP, throughput is {{c3::window / RTT}} and the extra bandwidth is unreachable.
Datacenter BDPs are tiny: $100$ Gb/s at $50\,\mu$s is only {{c4::625 kB}}, which is why switch buffers matter more than window size there.

concepts.L1: The quantity that decides whether a window is big enough. $\text{BDP} = B \times \text{RTT}$ is the capacity of the path viewed as a pipe; a sender must keep that many bytes unacknowledged to saturate it.
concepts.L2: BDP is why long-haul and in-datacenter tuning point in opposite directions. Across an ocean the BDP is hundreds of megabytes and the problem is windows too small; inside a rack it is hundreds of kilobytes and the problem is switch buffers far larger than the BDP, which adds queueing delay and no throughput.
concepts.L3: Derive the ceiling rather than looking it up. With no loss, a sender with window $W$ bytes and round-trip $R$ can have at most $W$ bytes outstanding, and must wait $R$ for the acknowledgement, so throughput is at most $W/R$. Setting $W/R = B$ and solving gives $W = B \times R$, the BDP. Everything follows. A 64 KiB window on a 100 ms path yields $65535 \times 8 / 0.1 = 5.24$ Mb/s regardless of a 10 Gb/s link, which is the pre-RFC-7323 ceiling. To fill 10 Gb/s at 100 ms you need 125 MB in flight, more than Linux autotunes to by default, and it takes roughly $\log_{2}(125\,\text{MB}/14.6\,\text{kB}) \approx 13$ round trips of slow start, or 1.3 seconds, just to reach that window.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute the bandwidth-delay product for {bw} Gb/s at {rtt} ms RTT, in megabytes, and state whether Linux's default tcp_rmem maximum of 6 MiB suffices. Answer with the bandwidth-delay product in bytes.
L4.answer: BDP_bytes = bw*1e9 * rtt/1000 / 8. 10 Gb/s at 100 ms = 125 MB, far above 6 MiB. 1 at 100 = 12.5 MB, above 6 MiB. 25 at 70 = 218.75 MB, far above. 100 at 0.05 ms = 0.625 MB, comfortably below. Long-haul high-bandwidth paths need explicit tcp_rmem raising; datacenter paths do not.
L4.explanation: The 6 MiB default was sized for the wide-area internet of a decade ago. It caps a 100 ms path at about 500 Mb/s, which is why bulk cross-region transfers stall well below link rate until tcp_rmem is raised or parallel streams are used.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the maximum throughput of a TCP connection with a fixed window of {w} bytes on an RTT of {rtt} ms, and derive how many slow-start round trips are needed to reach that window from an initial window of 10 segments of 1460 bytes. Answer with the maximum throughput in bits per second.
L4.explanation: Two separate limits fall out of the same model: the steady-state ceiling is window over RTT, and the time to reach it is logarithmic because slow start doubles cwnd each round trip. Short transfers are usually governed by the second, not the first.

prereqs: The sliding window and flow control

L0.body:
Two sane optimisations that together stall for 40 ms.

  Nagle (RFC 896):    hold a small segment while unacked small data
                      is outstanding; wait for the ACK.
  Delayed ACK (1122): hold the ACK, hoping to piggyback it on return
                      data. Linux caps the wait near 40 ms.

  write(header) -> sent (nothing outstanding)
  write(body)   -> HELD by Nagle, awaiting the ACK of header
  peer          -> HOLDS the ACK, awaiting data to piggyback
  40 ms later   -> delayed-ACK timer fires; body finally goes

  Fix: setsockopt(fd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &one, 4);
L0.cloze:
Nagle withholds a small segment while {{c1::unacknowledged}} small data is outstanding.
Delayed ACK withholds the acknowledgement hoping to {{c2::piggyback}} it on return data.
Together, on a write-write-read pattern, they produce a stall of about {{c3::40}} ms on Linux.
The correct fix is {{c4::TCP_NODELAY}}, or coalescing the two writes into a single writev.

concepts.L1: Nagle bounds the number of tiny segments in flight to one; delayed ACK bounds the number of pure ACKs. Each halves overhead in isolation. Composed on a request-response protocol they form a mutual wait broken only by a timer.
concepts.L2: TCP_NODELAY is not the real fix, it is the workaround for a bad write pattern. The application issued two writes for one logical message; coalescing them into one writev is strictly better, because it also removes a syscall and a segment. Reach for TCP_NODELAY when you cannot control the write pattern.
concepts.L3: The stall requires a specific shape: write, write, read, with the second write small and the peer having nothing to send until it has the whole message. The first write goes out because nothing is outstanding. The second is held by Nagle, which will not emit a sub-MSS segment while an unacknowledged small segment exists. The peer holds its ACK because delayed ACK waits for data to piggyback on, and it has no data because it has not received the complete request. Neither side is at fault and neither will act. Linux's delayed-ACK timer, capped near 40 ms, breaks it. The tell in a capture is a 40 ms gap with no loss and no retransmission, once per request, pinning latency regardless of load.

L4.prompt_tpl: An RPC client shows a latency floor of about {ms} ms per call on a 1 ms local path, with no loss and no retransmissions in the capture. Diagnose it and give two fixes, ranked.
L4.answer: Nagle interacting with the peer's delayed ACK, triggered by a write-write-read pattern: the header goes out, the body is held by Nagle awaiting an ACK, and the peer delays that ACK awaiting piggyback data it cannot produce until it has the body. The delayed-ACK timer near 40 ms breaks the deadlock. Best fix: coalesce the two writes into one writev or a single buffered write, which removes the small segment entirely. Second fix: setsockopt TCP_NODELAY, which disables Nagle for that socket.
L4.explanation: The signature is a constant, load-independent 40 ms floor with a clean capture. A latency floor that does not move with offered load is a timer, not congestion; the only question is which timer.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a {workload}, decide whether to set TCP_NODELAY and justify in terms of what Nagle actually protects against.
L4.answer: Bulk transfer: leave Nagle on; every write is already MSS-sized so Nagle never engages, and disabling it buys nothing. Latency-sensitive RPC: set TCP_NODELAY, and also fix the write pattern; the small-segment overhead Nagle prevents is irrelevant next to a 40 ms stall. Interactive SSH: this is Nagle's original target, one keystroke per packet with 40 bytes of header for 1 byte of data, but modern SSH sets TCP_NODELAY anyway because interactive latency matters more than the header ratio on links that are no longer 9600 baud.
L4.explanation: Nagle protects the network from a flood of 41-byte packets, a real 1984 problem. On modern links the header overhead it saves is negligible and the latency it costs is not, which is why almost every RPC framework sets TCP_NODELAY unconditionally.

prereqs: The sliding window and flow control

L0.body:
The side that closes FIRST enters TIME_WAIT and holds the 4-tuple for 2*MSL.

  active closer:  ESTABLISHED -> FIN_WAIT_1 -> FIN_WAIT_2 -> TIME_WAIT -> CLOSED
  passive closer: ESTABLISHED -> CLOSE_WAIT -> LAST_ACK    -> CLOSED

  Linux: TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN = 60 s, a compile-time constant in include/net/tcp.h.
  It is NOT tunable via sysctl. tcp_fin_timeout (this host: 60) is FIN_WAIT_2, not TIME_WAIT.

  Two jobs:
    1. absorb a retransmitted FIN so the peer's LAST_ACK completes
    2. let old duplicate segments for this 4-tuple die before it is reused
L0.cloze:
TIME_WAIT is entered by the side that closes {{c1::first}}, and lasts {{c2::2*MSL}}, which Linux fixes at 60 seconds.
Its two jobs are to absorb a retransmitted {{c3::FIN}} so the peer can finish closing, and to let stray duplicates from the old connection expire before the 4-tuple is reused.
On Linux the duration is a {{c4::compile-time}} constant, not a sysctl; tcp_fin_timeout controls FIN_WAIT_2 instead.

concepts.L1: The state a closing endpoint holds after the last ACK, keyed by the full 4-tuple. It exists so a lost final ACK can be recovered and so a reincarnated connection on the same 4-tuple cannot receive segments from the previous one.
concepts.L2: TIME_WAIT accumulating on a server means the server is closing connections first, which is usually the real bug. Clients should close. Enabling tcp_tw_reuse or, worse, the removed tcp_tw_recycle, treats the symptom and reintroduces exactly the hazard the state prevents.
concepts.L3: The reincarnation hazard is the half people forget. Suppose the 4-tuple (client:40122, server:443) is closed and immediately reused, and a segment from the old connection was delayed in a queue for 20 seconds. It carries a sequence number that, by chance, falls inside the new connection's window, and is accepted as data. TIME_WAIT prevents this by making the 4-tuple unusable for $2 \times \text{MSL}$, longer than any segment may survive. Operationally: closing 1000 connections per second holds $1000 \times 60 = 60000$ sockets in TIME_WAIT, cheap in memory but fatal to the ephemeral range (32768 to 60999, 28232 ports) for outbound connections to one destination.

L4.prompt_tpl: A host originates {rate} outbound connections per second to a single destination IP and port, closing each actively. With a 60-second TIME_WAIT and an ephemeral range of 32768-60999, compute the steady-state TIME_WAIT count and say whether ports are exhausted. Answer with the steady-state TIME_WAIT count.
L4.answer: count = rate * 60. Range size = 60999 - 32768 + 1 = 28232 ports. 500/s -> 30000 > 28232: exhausted. 1000/s -> 60000: badly exhausted. 200/s -> 12000: fits, with headroom. Exhaustion applies per destination 4-tuple, so spreading across destination IPs or ports multiplies the ceiling.
L4.explanation: The ceiling is range_size / TIME_WAIT seconds, about 470 connections per second per destination endpoint here. Beyond that, either stop closing actively (let the peer close), reuse connections, or widen the tuple space across destinations.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team proposes setting {knob} to clear TIME_WAIT sockets on a busy server. Evaluate the proposal and state what should be done instead.
L4.answer: All three attack the symptom. tcp_tw_reuse only permits reusing a TIME_WAIT socket for a new outbound connection when timestamps prove the new connection is newer; it is comparatively safe but only helps the client side. tcp_tw_recycle dropped connections from clients behind NAT because it applied per-source-IP timestamp checks to hosts that legitimately have different clocks, and was removed from Linux in 4.12. Shortening TIME_WAIT requires a kernel rebuild and reintroduces the reincarnation and lost-final-ACK hazards. The real fix: have the client close first, and reuse connections so fewer are opened.
L4.explanation: High TIME_WAIT on a server is a design signal, not a tuning problem. It says the server is the active closer, which also means the server pays the state cost for every short-lived connection it is asked to serve.

prereqs: The three-way handshake and its cost in RTTs

sections.note: Congestion control is a distributed control loop with no explicit feedback channel. Every algorithm here is a different guess about what the network is telling you.

L0.body:
cwnd starts at IW (RFC 6928: 10 segments) and DOUBLES every RTT.

  RTT 0:  cwnd = 10    (14.6 kB with MSS 1460)
  RTT 1:  cwnd = 20
  RTT 2:  cwnd = 40
  RTT n:  cwnd = 10 * 2^n

  Mechanism: on each ACK, cwnd += MSS. One window of ACKs doubles cwnd.
  Exit: cwnd >= ssthresh, or loss.

  RTTs to reach W segments = ceil(log2(W/10)).
  To fill 10 Gb/s at 100 ms (125 MB, ~85600 segments): ceil(log2(8560)) = 14 RTTs = 1.4 s.
L0.cloze:
Slow start increases cwnd by one MSS per {{c1::ACK}}, which {{c2::doubles}} it every round trip.
The Linux initial window is {{c3::10}} segments, about 14.6 kB.
Reaching a window of $W$ segments takes $\lceil \log_{2}(W/10) \rceil$ round trips, so filling a 125 MB pipe takes {{c4::14}} RTTs.
It exits when cwnd reaches {{c5::ssthresh}} or a loss is detected.

concepts.L1: The exponential ramp a sender uses when it has no estimate of available capacity. cwnd doubles each round trip until something says stop, so it finds the bottleneck in logarithmic time rather than linear.
concepts.L2: Slow start is not slow; it is the fastest phase TCP has. The name refers to starting from a small window rather than blasting a full one, which is what caused the 1986 collapse. It is also where most short web transfers spend their entire life, never reaching steady state at all.
concepts.L3: The name confuses people because the growth is exponential, and the practical consequence follows from that. A 100 kB response is about 69 segments. From an initial window of 10 it takes $\lceil \log_{2}(6.9) \rceil = 3$ round trips to have a window that large, so the transfer completes in roughly 4 RTTs and never leaves slow start. Its duration is therefore set entirely by RTT, not bandwidth, which is the quantitative reason edge termination beats bandwidth upgrades for typical web objects. The same arithmetic gives the opposite regime: filling a 10 Gb/s, 100 ms path needs 125 MB in flight, 14 doublings, 1.4 s of ramp during which the link is mostly idle.

L4.prompt_tpl: With an initial window of 10 segments of {mss} bytes, compute the number of slow-start round trips needed before the sender can have {target} bytes in flight.
L4.answer: RTTs = ceil(log2(target/(10*mss))). mss=1460: target 125 MB -> 125e6/14600 = 8562 -> ceil(log2 8562) = 14. target 1 MiB -> 1048576/14600 = 71.8 -> ceil(log2 71.8) = 7. target 100 kB -> 6.85 -> 3. With mss=1448 the answers are the same at these sizes.
L4.explanation: Each round trip doubles cwnd, so the count is a base-2 logarithm and is remarkably insensitive to the exact MSS. This is why ramp time grows slowly with transfer size but linearly with RTT.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the total time to transfer a {size} byte object over an RTT of {rtt} ms on an effectively infinite-bandwidth link, assuming the transfer never leaves slow start and one RTT is spent on the request. Answer with the total transfer time in milliseconds.
L4.answer: Segments n = ceil(size/1460). Data can be sent in r round trips where 10*(2^r - 1) >= n, so r = ceil(log2(n/10 + 1)). Total = (1 + r) * RTT. size=100000: n=69, r=3, total 4 RTT = 300 ms at 75 ms. size=14600: n=10, r=1, total 2 RTT = 150 ms. size=1000000: n=685, r=7, total 8 RTT = 600 ms. At 20 ms these are 80, 40 and 160 ms.
L4.explanation: The cumulative form matters: after r round trips a sender has been able to send 10(2^r - 1) segments, not 10*2^r. Bandwidth does not appear anywhere in the answer, which is the point.

L0.body:
Additive increase, multiplicative decrease. Reno, per RTT:

  no loss:  cwnd += 1 MSS          (additive, +1 segment per RTT)
  loss:     cwnd *= 0.5           (multiplicative, halve)

  cwnd over time:      /|  /|  /|      sawtooth, mean about 0.75 * W_max
                      / | / | / |
                     /  |/  |/  |

  Why AIMD and not AIAD or MIMD? Chiu and Jain (1989): among linear
  controls with a binary congestion signal, only AIMD converges to a
  fair AND efficient allocation from any starting point.

  Throughput ~ MSS / (RTT * sqrt(p))  -- the Mathis equation.
L0.cloze:
Additive increase adds {{c1::one MSS per RTT}}; multiplicative decrease {{c2::halves}} cwnd on loss.
Chiu and Jain showed that of the linear schemes, only {{c3::AIMD}} converges to both fairness and efficiency.
The Mathis equation says throughput scales as $\text{MSS}/(\text{RTT}\sqrt{p})$, so at fixed loss rate throughput is {{c4::inversely}} proportional to RTT.
The average window over the sawtooth is about {{c5::0.75}} of the peak.

concepts.L1: The control law under classical TCP: probe capacity linearly, retreat geometrically when loss says you overshot. The asymmetry is deliberate and is what makes competing flows converge to an equal share.
concepts.L2: AIMD is fair only between flows sharing an RTT. The Mathis relation makes throughput inversely proportional to RTT at equal loss, so a 10 ms flow beats a 100 ms flow by roughly ten to one on the same bottleneck. RTT unfairness is structural, not a bug in any implementation.
concepts.L3: The convergence argument is geometric. Plot two flows' rates as a point in the plane. Additive increase moves it along a 45-degree line parallel to the fairness line $x_{1}=x_{2}$, preserving the absolute difference. Multiplicative decrease moves it along a line through the origin, preserving the ratio and so shrinking the difference. Repeating the cycle drives the difference to zero while the efficiency line holds the sum near capacity, so the point spirals into the fair, efficient corner. Additive decrease would preserve the difference forever; multiplicative increase would amplify it. That is Chiu and Jain 1989, and the only reason AI plus MD is the pairing used.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using the Mathis relation $T \approx M/(R\sqrt p)$, where $M$ is the MSS, $R$ the RTT and $p$ the loss rate, compute the ratio of throughputs for two Reno flows on a shared bottleneck with the same loss rate but RTTs of {r1} ms and {r2} ms. Answer with the throughput ratio.
L4.answer: Throughput is inversely proportional to RTT at equal p and MSS, so the ratio is r2/r1. 10 vs 100 -> the short-RTT flow gets 10x. 10 vs 150 -> 15x. 20 vs 100 -> 5x. 20 vs 150 -> 7.5x.
L4.explanation: This is RTT unfairness and it is inherent to loss-based AIMD: the window grows one segment per round trip, so a shorter round trip grows it faster. CUBIC was designed partly to reduce this by making growth depend on elapsed time rather than on ACK arrivals.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain, using the two-flow rate plane, why {alt} fails to converge to a fair allocation while additive-increase multiplicative-decrease succeeds.
L4.answer: Additive increase and additive decrease both move the state point along 45-degree lines, which preserve the absolute difference between the two flows' rates; the difference never shrinks, so any initial unfairness persists forever even though efficiency is achieved. Multiplicative increase with multiplicative decrease moves along lines through the origin in both phases, preserving the ratio; again the unfairness is never removed, and the increase phase amplifies any perturbation. Only AIMD mixes the two: increase preserves the difference, decrease shrinks it, so the difference decays geometrically.
L4.explanation: The key insight is that fairness requires the two phases to act on different invariants. One phase must preserve the difference and the other must preserve the ratio; that combination is the only one that reduces the difference while staying near capacity.

concepts.t: RTO, fast retransmit, and fast recovery

L0.body:
Two loss detectors, four orders of magnitude apart in cost.

  RTO (RFC 6298):   SRTT  = (1-a)*SRTT + a*R          a = 1/8
                    RTTVAR= (1-b)*RTTVAR + b*|SRTT-R| b = 1/4
                    RTO   = SRTT + max(G, 4*RTTVAR),  floor 200 ms (Linux)
                    On timeout: cwnd = 1, ssthresh = cwnd/2, RTO doubles.

  Fast retransmit:  3 duplicate ACKs -> retransmit immediately, ~1 RTT.
  Fast recovery:    do NOT drop to cwnd=1; ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = ssthresh.

  Modern Linux uses RACK-TLP (RFC 8985): time-based, reorder-tolerant.
L0.cloze:
The retransmission timeout is $\text{SRTT} + 4 \times \text{RTTVAR}$, with a Linux floor of {{c2::200}} ms.
Fast retransmit fires after {{c1::three}} duplicate ACKs, costing about one RTT instead of an RTO.
Fast recovery avoids collapsing cwnd to 1 by setting cwnd to {{c3::ssthresh}} instead.
An RTO is far more expensive than fast retransmit because it drops cwnd to {{c4::1}} and doubles the timer on each repeat.

concepts.L1: TCP detects loss two ways: an acknowledgement that never arrives (timeout) or acknowledgements that indicate a gap (duplicate ACKs). The timeout is conservative and expensive; the duplicate-ACK path is fast and is what keeps throughput up under normal loss.
concepts.L2: The four in $\text{RTO} = \text{SRTT} + 4\,\text{RTTVAR}$ is why RTO is so much larger than RTT. Jacobson added the variance term precisely because a mean-based timer fires spuriously whenever delay is bursty, and a spurious RTO both retransmits needlessly and destroys the window.
concepts.L3: The cost gap is the reason incast is catastrophic and ordinary loss is not. Fast retransmit needs three duplicate ACKs, which needs at least four segments in flight after the lost one; the recovery costs about one RTT and leaves cwnd at half. An RTO costs at minimum the Linux floor of 200 ms, which on a datacenter path with a 50 microsecond RTT is four thousand round trips of dead time, and it resets cwnd to one segment so the window must be rebuilt from scratch. So the question in any loss event is not how much was lost but whether enough remained in flight to trigger duplicate ACKs. A small window, a transfer's tail, or a synchronised many-to-one burst all fail that test.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given SRTT = {srtt} ms and RTTVAR = {rttvar} ms, compute the RFC 6298 RTO and state the value Linux would actually use. Answer with the RFC 6298 RTO in milliseconds.
L4.answer: RTO = SRTT + 4*RTTVAR, then clamped to a 200 ms minimum on Linux. srtt=40, rttvar=5 -> 60 ms -> Linux uses 200 ms (floor). srtt=0.05, rttvar=0.01 -> 0.09 ms -> Linux uses 200 ms. srtt=8, rttvar=2 -> 16 ms -> Linux uses 200 ms.
L4.explanation: On every one of these the computed RTO is below the floor, so the floor dominates. That 200 ms floor is the single most important number in datacenter TCP: it makes an RTO four thousand times more expensive than an RTT on a 50 microsecond path.

L4.prompt_tpl: A flow loses one segment while {inflight} segments are in flight. State whether fast retransmit fires, the recovery cost, and what happens if it does not.
L4.answer: Fast retransmit needs three duplicate ACKs, hence at least three segments arriving after the lost one. With 10 in flight it fires: recovery costs roughly one RTT and cwnd falls to about half. With 4 in flight there are 3 segments after the loss, so it just fires. With 2 or 1 there are not enough segments to generate three duplicate ACKs, so detection falls through to the RTO, costing at least 200 ms on Linux and resetting cwnd to 1.
L4.explanation: This is why tail loss is disproportionately painful and why RFC 8985 adds Tail Loss Probe: the last segments of a transfer have nothing behind them to generate duplicate ACKs, so they always time out under classical rules.

L0.body:
RFC 9438. Default on Linux, Windows and Apple. Window is a function of TIME,
not of ACK arrivals:

  W(t) = C(t - K)^3 + W_max      C = 0.4,  beta = 0.7
  K = cbrt(W_max * (1 - beta) / C)

  W_max = 1000 segments:
    K       = cbrt(1000*0.3/0.4) = 9.086 s
    W(0)    = 0.7 * 1000 = 700          (just after the loss)
    W(K/2)  = 962.5
    W(K)    = 1000                      (back at W_max, plateau)
    W(2K)   = 1300                      (probing above)

  Reno-friendly region: if the cubic window is below Reno's, use Reno's.
L0.cloze:
CUBIC's window is a cubic function of {{c1::time}} since the last loss, not of acknowledgements, which makes it independent of RTT.
The multiplicative decrease factor is {{c2::0.7}}, gentler than Reno's 0.5.
The inflection point $K = \sqrt[3]{W_{\max}(1-\beta)/C}$ is where the window returns to {{c3::W_max}}.
Growth is {{c4::concave}} below $W_{\max}$ (cautious approach) and convex above it (aggressive probing).

concepts.L1: A loss-based algorithm whose window follows a cubic curve in wall-clock time since the last congestion event, with an inflection at the previous maximum. It approaches the old peak cautiously and probes past it aggressively.
concepts.L2: Making growth depend on time rather than on ACKs is the whole point: it removes the RTT unfairness of Reno, where a short-RTT flow grows its window faster simply because its ACKs return sooner. Two CUBIC flows with very different RTTs converge far closer to an equal share than two Reno flows do.
concepts.L3: The shape encodes a hypothesis about where capacity is. Just after a loss the algorithm believes $W_{\max}$ was roughly capacity, so the concave region near $K$ lingers close to $W_{\max}$, gathering evidence at the interesting window size. Beyond $K$ the convex region treats that estimate as stale and probes upward fast. With $W_{\max}=1000$, $C=0.4$ and $\beta = 0.7$: $K = \sqrt[3]{1000 \times 0.3/0.4} = 9.09$ s, $W(0)=700$, $W(K/2)=962.5$, $W(K)=1000$, $W(2K)=1300$. Recovery from 700 back to 1000 takes 9 seconds regardless of RTT: that decoupling is the design, and it makes CUBIC less aggressive than Reno on short-RTT paths.

L4.prompt_tpl: For CUBIC with $C=0.4$, $\beta = 0.7$ and $W_{{\max}} = {wmax}$ segments, compute $K$ in seconds and the window at $t = 2K$. Answer with K in seconds.
L4.explanation: W(2K) = 1.3*Wmax falls out algebraically because C*(2K-K)^3 = C*K^3 = Wmax*(1-beta) = 0.3*Wmax. The window is always 30 percent above the old peak one inflection-period after it, whatever the peak was.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two flows share a bottleneck with RTTs of {r1} ms and {r2} ms. Compare how unequally CUBIC and Reno divide the link, and explain the mechanism responsible.
L4.answer: Reno's window grows one segment per round trip, so growth rate is proportional to 1/RTT and throughput ends up roughly proportional to 1/RTT; the 10 ms flow takes about ten (or twenty) times the share. CUBIC's window is a function of elapsed wall-clock time since the last loss, so both flows traverse the same cubic curve at the same real-time rate regardless of how often their ACKs return, and their shares converge much closer to equal. The mechanism is precisely the substitution of a wall-clock argument for an ACK-driven one.
L4.explanation: CUBIC does not achieve exact RTT fairness, because the long-RTT flow still reacts to loss later, but replacing ACK-clocked growth with time-clocked growth removes the dominant term. This was one of the two stated design goals in the original paper, alongside scaling to high-BDP paths.

L0.body:
Model-based, not loss-based. Estimate two things and pace to them:

  BtlBw   max delivery rate observed over the last ~10 RTTs
  RTprop  min RTT observed over the last ~10 s
  BDP     = BtlBw * RTprop
  cwnd    = 2 * BDP  (cap), pacing rate = pacing_gain * BtlBw

  States: STARTUP -> DRAIN -> PROBE_BW -> PROBE_RTT
  PROBE_BW cycles pacing_gain over 1.25, 0.75, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1
  PROBE_RTT drops cwnd to 4 packets for 200 ms to re-measure RTprop.

  Loss is NOT the congestion signal. BBRv3 is at the IETF as
  draft-ietf-ccwg-bbr (draft 06, July 2026).
L0.cloze:
BBR estimates bottleneck bandwidth {{c1::BtlBw}} and minimum round-trip propagation time {{c2::RTprop}}, and paces at their product.
Unlike Reno and CUBIC it does not treat {{c3::loss}} as the congestion signal.
PROBE_BW raises the pacing gain to {{c4::1.25}} to probe for more bandwidth, then to 0.75 to drain what it queued.
PROBE_RTT periodically shrinks cwnd to re-measure RTprop, because a persistently full queue would otherwise {{c5::hide}} the true minimum RTT.

concepts.L1: A congestion control that builds an explicit model of the path, maximum delivery rate and minimum round-trip time, and sends at that rate rather than inferring capacity from packet loss. Cardwell and colleagues at Google, 2016.
concepts.L2: BBR's contribution is not speed, it is decoupling congestion from loss. On paths with non-congestive loss CUBIC collapses its window at every random drop; BBR does not, since a drop is not evidence about BtlBw. The cost is that BBRv1 could be unfair to CUBIC; v2 and v3 add loss and ECN response.
concepts.L3: Kleinrock showed in 1979 that the optimum is where delivery rate is maximised and queueing delay minimised, the moment in-flight data equals the BDP. Loss-based control cannot sit there: it learns it has overshot only by overflowing the buffer, so it operates at BDP plus buffer, filling the queue by design. BBR aims at the optimum by measuring both coordinates. The catch is that the two cannot be measured at once: maximising rate fills the pipe and inflates RTT, while measuring RTprop needs an empty queue. BBR alternates instead, taking BtlBw as a windowed maximum and RTprop as a windowed minimum, with PROBE_RTT forcing a drain.

L4.prompt_tpl: A long-haul path has a random, non-congestive loss rate of {p}. Compare BBR and CUBIC throughput qualitatively and explain the mechanism.
L4.answer: CUBIC treats every loss as congestion and multiplicatively reduces the window, so its steady-state throughput follows roughly MSS/(RTT*sqrt(p)); at 1 percent loss on a long RTT this is a small fraction of link capacity even though the link is idle. BBR does not reduce its rate in response to loss alone: it paces to its measured BtlBw, and a random drop does not lower the observed delivery rate much, so throughput stays near capacity. The mechanism is that BBR's control variable is a measured rate, whereas CUBIC's is a window driven by a loss signal that conflates corruption with congestion.
L4.explanation: This is BBR's clearest practical win and why Google deployed it on long-haul traffic first. It is also the fairness complaint: on a shallow-buffered bottleneck shared with CUBIC, BBRv1 can take more than its share precisely because it ignores the loss CUBIC is obeying.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why BBR cannot measure BtlBw and RTprop simultaneously, and how PROBE_RTT with a {ms} ms window resolves it.
L4.answer: Measuring maximum delivery rate requires enough data in flight to keep the bottleneck busy, which necessarily builds some queue and inflates measured RTT; measuring true propagation delay requires an empty queue, which means sending below capacity and understating the rate. They are conflicting operating points. BBR resolves it in time rather than simultaneously: BtlBw is a maximum over a window of about ten RTTs, RTprop a minimum over about ten seconds, and PROBE_RTT deliberately drops cwnd to four packets for 200 ms so the queue drains and a clean minimum can be observed.
L4.explanation: The 200 ms is chosen to exceed one round trip on essentially any path so the queue actually drains, while being short enough that the throughput cost, roughly 2 percent of time, is acceptable. Synchronising PROBE_RTT across flows was an explicit design goal so they drain together.

L0.body:
A 1 Gb/s uplink with a 128 MB buffer, filled by a loss-based sender:

  drain = 128e6 * 8 / 1e9 = 1.024 s of standing QUEUE

  Every packet behind it -- a DNS query, an SSH keystroke -- waits a
  second. Bandwidth is fine. Latency is destroyed.

  CoDel (Nichols and Jacobson): track the MINIMUM sojourn time over a
  100 ms interval; if it stays above 5 ms, start dropping. Measures TIME
  in queue, not LENGTH -- length says nothing about delay.

  ECN (RFC 3168): mark CE instead of dropping; the receiver echoes ECE
  and the sender reacts as if to loss. A signal without loss.
L0.cloze:
Bufferbloat is excess {{c1::latency}} caused by oversized buffers that a loss-based sender fills before it sees any signal.
A 128 MB buffer draining at 1 Gb/s holds about {{c2::1}} second of queue.
CoDel triggers on the minimum {{c3::sojourn time}} over an interval rather than on queue length, because length alone does not determine delay.
{{c4::ECN}} lets a router signal congestion by marking a packet instead of dropping it.

concepts.L1: Oversized unmanaged buffers convert congestion into delay instead of loss. Loss-based congestion control needs loss to back off, so it fills whatever buffer exists, and a large buffer means seconds of standing queue on an otherwise healthy link.
concepts.L2: The bug is the interaction, not the buffer. Memory got cheap and vendors sized buffers generously to avoid drops, which looked like a strict improvement. But a loss-based sender treats absence of loss as permission to send more, so the buffer is not a shock absorber, it is a target the sender will always hit.
concepts.L3: Two derivations. First, why length is the wrong metric: 100 queued packets is 120 microseconds on a 10 Gb/s link and 1.2 seconds on a 1 Mb/s link. Only sojourn time is comparable across links, which is why CoDel measures how long packets actually waited. Second, why the minimum and not the mean: a burst through a briefly non-empty queue is harmless, and the queue drains. A standing queue never empties, so its minimum sojourn time over an interval is nonzero. CoDel drops only when that minimum exceeds 5 ms for 100 ms, separating a good queue from a bad one with no configuration and no knowledge of link rate. ECN is the complement: the same signal without discarding the packet.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {rate} link has a {buf} MB unmanaged buffer that a bulk transfer fills. Compute the worst-case queueing delay it adds to an unrelated interactive packet.
L4.answer: delay = buffer_bits / rate_bps = buf*8e6/rate. 1 Gb/s with 128 MB: 1.024 s. 1 Gb/s with 32 MB: 0.256 s. 100 Mb/s with 128 MB: 10.24 s. 100 Mb/s with 8 MB: 0.64 s. 10 Gb/s with 128 MB: 0.1024 s. 10 Gb/s with 8 MB: 6.4 ms.
L4.explanation: The same buffer is catastrophic on a slow link and nearly harmless on a fast one, which is why buffers must be sized in time, not bytes. This is also why a home router hurts far more than a datacenter switch with the same memory.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why CoDel uses the {stat} sojourn time over an interval rather than the instantaneous queue length, and what would go wrong with the alternative.
L4.answer: Queue length is not comparable across link rates: 100 packets is microseconds on a fast link and seconds on a slow one, so any length threshold must be hand-tuned per link and will be wrong when the rate changes. Sojourn time is directly the quantity that harms applications. The minimum rather than the mean is used because a transient burst produces a queue that drains, which is a queue doing its job; only a queue that never empties has a nonzero minimum sojourn time over the interval. Using the mean or the instantaneous value would penalise harmless bursts and make the algorithm drop traffic it should absorb.
L4.explanation: This is what makes CoDel parameterless in practice: 5 ms target and 100 ms interval work across link rates from dial-up to 10 Gb/s, because the measured quantity is already normalised by rate.

L0.body:
N workers answer one request simultaneously. Their responses collide in the
last-hop switch buffer.

  40 senders x 64 kB       = 2.56 MB arriving in one RTT
  ToR buffer for that port = 512 kB
  -> overflow; each sender has too little in flight for 3 dup ACKs
  -> RTO, floored at 200 ms on Linux
  -> a 50 us RTT becomes 200 ms: a 4000x latency cliff

DCTCP (Alizadeh et al., SIGCOMM 2010; RFC 8257):
  mark CE when the INSTANTANEOUS queue > K (~65 pkts at 10 Gb/s)
  alpha = (1-g)*alpha + g*F   F = fraction of ACKs marked, g = 1/16
  cwnd  = cwnd * (1 - alpha/2)   -- reduce IN PROPORTION
L0.cloze:
Incast is many synchronised senders overflowing one {{c1::shallow}} switch buffer at the last hop.
It is catastrophic rather than gradual because each flow is too small to trigger {{c2::fast retransmit}}, so loss falls through to the RTO with its {{c3::200}} ms Linux floor.
DCTCP marks ECN when the instantaneous queue exceeds a threshold $K$ and reduces cwnd by $\alpha/2$, where $\alpha$ estimates the {{c4::fraction}} of marked acknowledgements.
Unlike Reno, DCTCP's reduction is {{c5::proportional}} to the extent of congestion rather than always a half.

concepts.L1: The pathology of partition-aggregate workloads: many servers reply to one client at once, the last-hop buffer overflows, and the resulting loss is detected by timeout rather than by duplicate ACKs. Throughput falls off a cliff as the fan-in grows.
concepts.L2: Incast is not a bandwidth problem and capacity does not fix it. The traffic is a microburst well within link rate on average; the failure is that a synchronised burst exceeds the buffer inside one RTT, and the recovery that fires is four thousand times slower than the network.
concepts.L3: DCTCP's departure from Reno is the proportional reduction. Reno halves cwnd on any signal, which on a datacenter path throws away most of a small window for a queue barely over threshold. DCTCP instead tracks $\alpha$, an EWMA of the marked-ACK fraction with $g=1/16$, and applies $\text{cwnd} \leftarrow \text{cwnd}(1-\alpha/2)$. If every ACK is marked, $\alpha \to 1$ and the cut is a half, exactly Reno. If one eighth are marked, $\alpha \approx 0.125$ and cwnd falls about 6 percent. The queue is then short and stable rather than sawtoothing, leaving headroom for the next incast burst. Marking on the instantaneous queue is deliberate: the signal must arrive inside one RTT to be useful.

L4.prompt_tpl: {n} servers each send a {sz} kB response to one client simultaneously through a switch port with a {buf} kB buffer. Compute the bytes arriving in one burst and state whether the buffer overflows. Answer with the burst size in kB.
L4.answer: burst = n*sz kB. 40x64 = 2560 kB, overflows both 512 and 1024 kB. 20x32 = 640 kB, overflows 512, fits in 1024. 100x64 = 6400 kB, overflows both. 40x32 = 1280 kB, overflows both. 100x32 = 3200 kB, overflows both. 20x64 = 1280 kB, overflows both.
L4.explanation: The fan-in multiplies, the buffer does not. This is why incast is a scaling cliff: doubling the worker count doubles the burst, while the buffer is fixed by the switch ASIC, typically 10-20 MB shared across all ports on a modern ToR.

L4.prompt_tpl: For DCTCP with $g = 1/16$, derive the steady-state cwnd multiplier when the fraction of marked ACKs converges to {f}, and compare with Reno. Answer with the cwnd multiplier.
L4.answer: In steady state alpha converges to F, and cwnd is multiplied by 1 - alpha/2. F=1.0 -> alpha=1, multiplier 0.5, identical to Reno. F=0.5 -> multiplier 0.75, a 25 percent reduction. F=0.125 -> multiplier 0.9375, a 6.25 percent reduction. Reno applies 0.5 in every case regardless of how congested the link is.
L4.explanation: The EWMA with g=1/16 makes alpha converge to F over roughly 16 windows, so the reduction tracks sustained congestion and ignores single marks. Reno's fixed half is the reason a shallow datacenter queue produces a deep throughput sawtooth for no benefit.
