sections.note: QUIC is the answer to a question TCP could no longer be asked: how do you change a transport that middleboxes have frozen?

concepts.t: UDP, and when it is the right answer

L0.body:
UDP gives you exactly four things beyond raw IP:

  16-bit source port, 16-bit destination port, 16-bit length, 16-bit checksum

That is the whole header: 8 bytes. No connection, no ordering, no
retransmission, no congestion control, no flow control.

  sendto(fd, buf, n, 0, (struct sockaddr*)&dst, sizeof dst);

Datagram boundaries ARE preserved: one sendto -> one recvfrom, or nothing.
Right when you need: multiplexing without a handshake (DNS), your own
loss policy (video, games), or a transport of your own (QUIC).
L0.cloze:
The UDP header is {{c1::8}} bytes: source port, destination port, length, checksum.
Unlike TCP, UDP {{c2::preserves}} datagram boundaries, so one sendto maps to one recvfrom.
It supplies no ordering, no retransmission and no {{c3::congestion control}}, so anything built on it must supply its own.
It is the right choice when the application's {{c4::loss policy}} differs from retransmit-everything, or when you are building your own transport.

concepts.L1: IP plus ports plus a checksum. UDP adds demultiplexing to a host's addressing and nothing else. Every reliability property TCP provides must be reimplemented above it, which is precisely why it is the substrate for new transports.
concepts.L2: The reason to choose UDP is almost never speed. It is that TCP's retransmit-everything-in-order policy is wrong for the application: a video frame that arrives late is useless, and stalling later frames to deliver it makes things worse. UDP moves the loss policy into the application, where the semantics live.
concepts.L3: UDP obliges you to answer the questions TCP answered for you, and the skipped one is congestion control. An application sending at a fixed rate regardless of loss contributes to collapse and at scale is indistinguishable from an attack; RFC 8085 makes circuit-breaker behaviour a requirement. The second obligation is amplification: a service answering a small query with a large response over UDP is a reflector, because the source address is unverified. A 60-byte query and a 4000-byte DNSSEC response is roughly 66x amplification. Hence response rate limiting, DNS cookies, and QUIC's rule that a server may not send more than three times the bytes received until the address is validated.

L4.prompt_tpl: Choose TCP or UDP for {app}, and state which specific TCP property is the deciding factor.
L4.answer: Real-time voice: UDP. The deciding property is in-order delivery; a retransmitted 20 ms frame arrives after its playout deadline and blocks the frames behind it, so late data is worse than lost data. DNS resolver: UDP for the common case, because a query and response fit in one datagram and a handshake would triple the latency; fall back to TCP when the response exceeds the path MTU or truncation is signalled. Bulk log shipping: TCP, because every byte matters and the retransmit-everything policy is exactly right. Game position stream: UDP, because only the newest position matters and an old one should be discarded, not retransmitted.
L4.explanation: The test is always the same: if a late byte is still useful, TCP's policy is right. If a late byte is worthless or actively harmful, TCP will spend bandwidth and latency delivering it anyway, and the loss policy belongs in the application.

L4.prompt_tpl: Review a UDP service that answers a {qsize}-byte request with a {rsize}-byte response. Compute the amplification factor and name the required mitigations.
L4.answer: Amplification factor = rsize/qsize. 4000/60 = 66.7x, 512/60 = 8.5x, 3000/40 = 75x. Because UDP does not validate the source address, an attacker spoofs the victim's address and the service delivers that multiple of the attack traffic to the victim. Mitigations: response rate limiting per source prefix; requiring proof of address ownership before sending a large response (DNS cookies, or QUIC's rule that a server may not send more than three times the bytes received until validation); and network-level BCP 38 source address filtering upstream.
L4.explanation: The three-times rule in QUIC is the general form of this mitigation and worth remembering: bound the response to a small multiple of what you have received from an unvalidated address, so the protocol is never a useful amplifier.

L0.body:
QUIC (RFC 9000) is a complete transport inside UDP, run by the application.

  Out of the kernel: streams, loss recovery, congestion control,
                     flow control, connection state.
  Into encryption:   nearly the whole header; only the connection ID
                     stays visible to the network.

  TCP + TLS 1.3       QUIC
   SYN                 Initial (carries ClientHello)
   SYN-ACK             Initial+Handshake (ServerHello, cert)
   ACK + ClientHello   Handshake fin + 1-RTT data
   2 RTT to data       1 RTT; 0 with resumption

  Loss on stream 3 does not block stream 5.
L0.cloze:
QUIC runs over {{c1::UDP}} and implements streams, loss recovery and congestion control in {{c2::userspace}} rather than the kernel.
It merges the transport and cryptographic handshakes, reaching data in {{c3::1}} RTT instead of TCP plus TLS 1.3's 2.
Because each stream is ordered {{c4::independently}}, loss on one stream does not stall the others.
Connections survive an address change because they are identified by a {{c5::connection ID}} rather than by the 4-tuple.

concepts.L1: A transport with TCP's guarantees, carried in UDP datagrams, implemented above the kernel and encrypted almost end to end. It exists because middleboxes made TCP unchangeable, not because UDP is faster.
concepts.L2: Header encryption is the load-bearing design decision, not a privacy feature. TCP could not be extended because middleboxes rejected headers they did not recognise; QUIC encrypts its header so no middlebox can parse it, which is the only way to keep a transport evolvable.
concepts.L3: Two consequences follow from userspace. First, per-packet cost rises: a QUIC endpoint crosses the syscall boundary per datagram and encrypts in userspace, so early deployments burned two to three times kernel TCP's CPU per byte. Hence the importance of GSO, GRO and sendmmsg in QUIC stacks. Second, deployment velocity inverts: a browser and a CDN can ship a congestion-control change to hundreds of millions of endpoints in weeks, where TCP needed a decade of kernel adoption on both ends. The connection ID gives the visible benefit: a phone moving from Wi-Fi to cellular changes its IP, killing every TCP connection, while a QUIC connection continues over a new 4-tuple.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare time to first response byte over a {rtt} ms path for TCP+TLS1.3+HTTP/2, QUIC with a full handshake, and QUIC with 0-RTT resumption. Answer with the QUIC 1-RTT time in milliseconds.
L4.answer: TCP+TLS1.3 = 3 RTT; QUIC 1-RTT = 2 RTT; QUIC 0-RTT = 1 RTT. At 75 ms: 225, 150, 75 ms. At 150 ms: 450, 300, 150. At 30 ms: 90, 60, 30. QUIC saves one round trip by merging the transport and cryptographic handshakes, and a second by sending application data in the first flight on resumption.
L4.explanation: The saving is one to two round trips, always, independent of bandwidth. It is largest exactly where it matters most: long paths and small responses, which is most of the web.

L4.prompt_tpl: A mobile client moves from Wi-Fi to cellular mid-download, changing its {what}. Contrast what happens to a TCP connection and a QUIC connection, and name the mechanism responsible.
L4.answer: The TCP connection is identified by the 4-tuple, so changing the source address makes every subsequent segment belong to a connection neither endpoint has; the server sends RST or silently drops, and the client must re-handshake, re-negotiate TLS, and restart congestion control from the initial window. QUIC identifies the connection by a connection ID carried in the header, independent of addresses, so the server matches the datagram to the existing connection state and continues, keeping the congestion window and the encryption keys. This is connection migration, RFC 9000 section 9.
L4.explanation: QUIC still validates the new path before sending much on it, using a PATH_CHALLENGE round trip and a temporary congestion-window reduction, so migration is not entirely free; but it preserves the session, the keys and most of the state.

L0.body:
0-RTT sends application data in the FIRST flight, before the handshake completes,
encrypted with a key derived from a previous session (TLS 1.3 PSK, RFC 8446 s2.3).

  client -> ClientHello + early_data: "POST /transfer {amount: 100}"
  server -> ... accepts, processes ...

An attacker who captured that flight can REPLAY it verbatim: there is no
server nonce in the first flight, so nothing binds it to one exchange.

Rule (RFC 8446 s8, RFC 9001 s9.2): 0-RTT data must be idempotent.
GET yes. POST /transfer no. CDNs allow 0-RTT for GET and HEAD only.
L0.cloze:
0-RTT sends application data in the {{c1::first}} flight, encrypted under a key derived from a previous session, saving one round trip.
It is replayable because the first flight contains no {{c2::server}} nonce to bind it to a single exchange.
The rule is that 0-RTT data must be {{c3::idempotent}}; in practice servers restrict it to GET and HEAD.
It also loses {{c4::forward secrecy}} for the early data, since the key comes from the previous session's PSK.

concepts.L1: Resumption that carries application data in the client's very first packet, using a pre-shared key from an earlier session. It removes the last round trip before data and is the fastest handshake in deployment.
concepts.L2: The replay risk is structural, not an implementation bug. Anti-replay caches help within one server but cannot span an anycast fleet without shared state, so the guarantee degrades to at-most-once-per-datacenter. Hence the specification pushes the requirement up to the application.
concepts.L3: Trace why a nonce cannot fix it. In a normal handshake the server contributes fresh randomness and the client's data is encrypted under a key derived from both contributions, so a captured flight cannot be replayed into another session. In 0-RTT the client has not heard from the server, by definition, so the early-data key derives only from the stored PSK and the client's own randomness. An attacker who records the flight resends it; the server decrypts and processes it identically. Mitigations are partial: single-use tickets need fleet-wide state, and a timestamp window narrows but never closes the gap. The workable rule is the RFCs': restrict 0-RTT to requests whose repetition is harmless.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team enables 0-RTT for all HTTP methods to cut latency, arguing their anti-replay cache makes it safe across {n} datacenters. Evaluate.
L4.answer: Unsafe. An anti-replay cache is per-server or at best per-datacenter; making it correct across n datacenters requires a synchronous global consensus check on every 0-RTT request, which costs at least a round trip and therefore destroys the entire benefit of 0-RTT. Without that, an attacker replays the captured flight to a different datacenter, whose cache has never seen it, and the request executes again. For POST and other state-changing methods this means duplicated transactions. The correct policy is to accept 0-RTT only for idempotent methods and to reject early data for everything else, forcing those requests to the 1-RTT path.
L4.explanation: The argument that kills it is a latency one: any replay defence strong enough to be safe requires coordination whose cost exceeds the round trip 0-RTT was saving. This is why the RFCs put the requirement on the application rather than on the server implementation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain precisely why {mech} cannot be used to prevent 0-RTT replay, in terms of what the client knows when it sends early data.
L4.answer: Because the client sends early data before receiving anything from the server in this session. A server nonce must be delivered by the server, which requires a round trip, and the whole point of 0-RTT is to avoid that round trip. The early-data key can therefore only be derived from the stored PSK and the client's own randomness, both of which are contained in the captured flight, so replaying that flight reproduces exactly the same decryption on the server. The circularity is fundamental: any freshness the server contributes costs the round trip 0-RTT exists to eliminate.
L4.explanation: This is the general shape of the tradeoff: freshness against an off-path attacker requires at least one message from the party you are proving freshness to. 0-RTT trades exactly that guarantee for exactly that round trip.

1.1 (RFC 9112)  2 (RFC 9113)     3 (RFC 9114)
  transport    TCP             TCP              QUIC over UDP
  concurrency  ~6 conns/origin 1 conn, streams  1 conn, streams
  head-of-line per connection  at the TCP layer none across streams
  headers      plain text      HPACK binary     QPACK binary

HTTP/2 fixed application-layer HOL blocking and left transport HOL alone:
one lost TCP segment stalls EVERY multiplexed stream, because TCP delivers
bytes in order and cannot see stream boundaries. HTTP/3 removes the residue.
L0.cloze:
HTTP/1.1 achieves concurrency by opening about {{c1::6}} connections per origin; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over {{c2::one}} connection.
HTTP/2 removes head-of-line blocking at the {{c3::application}} layer but not at the transport layer, because TCP still delivers a single ordered byte stream.
A single lost segment therefore stalls {{c4::every}} HTTP/2 stream on that connection.
HTTP/3 removes the residue by running over {{c5::QUIC}}, whose streams are ordered independently.

concepts.L1: Three versions of one protocol distinguished mainly by how they achieve concurrency. 1.1 opens many connections, 2 multiplexes over one TCP connection, 3 multiplexes over QUIC where the streams are genuinely independent.
concepts.L2: HTTP/2 can be slower than HTTP/1.1 on a lossy path, and this surprises people. Six HTTP/1.1 connections mean a lost segment stalls one sixth of the requests; one HTTP/2 connection means it stalls all of them. Multiplexing concentrated the exposure, which is exactly what HTTP/3 was built to undo.
concepts.L3: Head-of-line blocking exists at three layers and each version addresses a different one. At the application layer, HTTP/1.1 could not start response two until response one finished; HTTP/2's frames fixed that. At the transport layer, TCP presents one in-order byte stream, so a lost segment holds back every byte behind it, including bytes of other HTTP/2 streams that arrived fine; the kernel cannot skip ahead, not knowing where stream boundaries lie. QUIC tracks per-stream offsets, so a gap in stream 3 blocks only stream 3. At the switch, a shared input buffer blocks a packet bound for an idle output behind one bound for a busy port; virtual output queueing fixes it. One name, three fixes.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a path with {loss} packet loss and 100 ms RTT, compare expected performance of HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 for a page of 80 small objects.
L4.answer: At zero loss HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 both beat 1.1 clearly: one handshake instead of six, one congestion window that grows once, and header compression on 80 requests. At 1 percent loss the ranking changes: every lost segment stalls all HTTP/2 streams at the TCP layer, while HTTP/1.1's six connections isolate the damage to one sixth of the requests, so HTTP/2 can lose to 1.1. HTTP/3 keeps the multiplexing benefits and does not have the transport stall, so it wins in both regimes. At 0.1 percent loss HTTP/2 is still ahead of 1.1 because stalls are rare enough that the handshake and window savings dominate.
L4.explanation: The crossover exists because HTTP/2 traded fault isolation for efficiency. Whether that trade pays depends entirely on the loss rate, which is why HTTP/3 exists: it takes the efficiency without giving up the isolation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Name the three layers at which head-of-line blocking occurs and, for {layer}, state the mechanism and the fix.
L4.answer: The three layers are the application (HTTP/1.1 request serialisation), the transport (TCP's in-order byte stream), and the switch (a shared input buffer whose head packet is destined for a busy output). Transport: TCP delivers bytes in order and cannot know where HTTP/2 stream boundaries are, so one lost segment holds back later bytes for every stream; the fix is per-stream sequencing in the transport, which is what QUIC does. Application: HTTP/1.1 could not begin a second response before the first completed; the fix is framing and multiplexing, HTTP/2. Switch: a packet for an idle output waits behind one for a busy output; the fix is virtual output queueing, a separate queue per output port.
L4.explanation: The pattern is identical at all three: a single ordered queue serving multiple independent consumers. The fix is always the same in form, split the queue by consumer, and only differs in where you can afford to keep the state.

sections.t: TLS, and what it costs in round trips
sections.note: Encryption is cheap. The handshake is not. Everything in TLS 1.3 is an attempt to spend fewer round trips.

L0.body:
The server hands the client an encrypted blob; the client returns it to skip
the certificate exchange.

  full handshake -> server: NewSessionTicket { ticket, ticket_age_add,
                                               max_early_data_size }
  next connection -> ClientHello + pre_shared_key(ticket)
                  -> 1 RTT, or 0 RTT if early data is sent with it

The ticket is sealed under a Session Ticket Encryption Key (STEK) shared
by the fleet. Anyone holding the STEK can decrypt every session resumed
under it, so the rotation interval IS the forward-secrecy window.
L0.cloze:
A resumption ticket is an {{c1::encrypted}} blob of session state that the server hands the client, letting a later connection skip the certificate exchange.
The ticket is sealed under a {{c2::STEK}}, a key shared across the server fleet.
Because that key can decrypt every session resumed under it, the {{c3::rotation}} interval bounds forward secrecy for resumed sessions.
Resumption saves the certificate exchange; it does not by itself save a {{c4::round trip}} unless 0-RTT early data is also used.

concepts.L1: Stateless resumption: the server encrypts the session state and gives it to the client to hold, so no server-side session cache is needed and any server in the fleet can resume. The ticket is opaque to the client.
concepts.L2: Resumption without 0-RTT still costs one round trip; what it removes is the certificate transmission and the signature verification, which is CPU and bytes, not latency. People conflate the two and then blame resumption when latency does not improve.
concepts.L3: The STEK is quietly dangerous: it converts per-session forward secrecy into per-key forward secrecy. In a full handshake the ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys are discarded, so recorded traffic survives even a total server compromise. A resumed session's keys derive from the ticket, sealed under the STEK, so an attacker with the STEK and a recording decrypts every session resumed under it. The mitigation is rotation: rotate hourly, and the window is an hour. The failure mode is a fleet that shares the STEK to make tickets portable, distributes it widely, and rotates it rarely; deployments holding STEKs for months silently voided forward secrecy for most of their connections.

L4.prompt_tpl: A fleet shares one Session Ticket Encryption Key across all servers and rotates it every {period}. State the forward-secrecy exposure and the correct configuration.
L4.answer: An attacker who records traffic and later obtains the STEK can decrypt every session resumed under that key, so the exposure window equals the rotation period: 30 days, 7 days, or 1 hour respectively. The first two effectively void forward secrecy for most connections, since most connections resume. Correct configuration: rotate on the order of hours, keep at most one or two previous keys accepted for decryption so in-flight tickets still work, distribute keys over an authenticated channel, and hold them only in memory.
L4.explanation: Forward secrecy is a property of the whole system, not of the cipher suite. A perfect ephemeral handshake whose resumption tickets are sealed under a month-old shared key gives an attacker a month of retroactive decryption.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service sees {pct} of connections resume. Decide whether enabling resumption is worth it and state precisely what it saves and does not save.
L4.answer: It is worth enabling in all three cases, because the cost is one configuration item and the saving scales with the resumption rate. What it saves: transmitting the certificate chain, typically 2 to 4 kB, and the server's signature plus the client's chain verification, which is the dominant CPU cost of a TLS handshake. What it does not save on its own: a round trip. A resumed 1-RTT handshake is still one round trip, so latency improves only if 0-RTT early data is also enabled, which brings the replay constraints with it.
L4.explanation: Separate the two axes. Resumption is a bandwidth and CPU optimisation; 0-RTT is the latency optimisation, and only 0-RTT carries the replay risk. Enabling resumption alone is uncontroversial.

L0.cloze:
listen()'s backlog argument sizes the {{c1::accept}} queue, not the SYN queue, and is clamped by {{c2::somaxconn}}.
The SYN queue holds {{c3::half-open}} connections and is sized by tcp_max_syn_backlog.
A connection moves from the SYN queue to the accept queue when the {{c4::final ACK}} arrives.
When the accept queue overflows the kernel drops the ACK silently, and the counter to watch is {{c5::ListenOverflows}}.

concepts.L1: Four calls make a server: create a socket, claim an address, mark it passive with a backlog, then remove one established connection per accept. The backlog is the depth of the queue of connections the kernel has handshaked but the application has not taken.
concepts.L2: The backlog does not limit concurrent connections, only how many may sit completed and unaccepted. Raising it does not increase capacity; it increases the queue in front of a server that is already too slow, converting refusals into latency. An overflowing accept queue means the accept loop is not running often enough.
concepts.L3: The split exists because the server allocates state on SYN, before the peer has proved it can receive. A SYN flood fills that queue with half-open entries from spoofed addresses, and real SYNs are dropped. SYN cookies remove the state: the server encodes the half-open connection into the initial sequence number of its SYN-ACK, a keyed hash of the 4-tuple and a coarse timestamp. If the client's ACK returns that number plus one, the server rebuilds the connection from the cookie alone. The cost is that options living in that state, notably window scaling and SACK, are constrained, so cookies are a fallback under pressure rather than the default path. That is what tcp_syncookies=1 does.

L4.prompt_tpl: A server sets listen backlog to {bl} while net.core.somaxconn is 128, and drops connections under load. State the effective backlog, the counter that confirms the diagnosis, and the correct fix.
L4.answer: The effective accept-queue depth is min(backlog, somaxconn) = 128 in all three cases; the large listen() argument is silently clamped. Confirm with the ListenOverflows and ListenDrops counters in /proc/net/netstat (nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows), which increment on each dropped completed connection. The fix is twofold: raise net.core.somaxconn so the value actually takes effect, and, more importantly, find why the accept loop is not draining the queue, because a persistently full accept queue means the application is the bottleneck and a deeper queue only adds latency before the same failure.
L4.explanation: The silent clamping is the trap: listen() does not fail or warn, so the code looks correct. Always verify the effective value rather than the requested one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain how SYN cookies allow a server to complete a handshake without holding SYN-queue state, and name the specific cost of doing so.
L4.answer: Instead of storing the half-open connection, the server encodes it into the initial sequence number it sends in the SYN-ACK: a keyed hash over the 4-tuple, a coarse timestamp, and an index into a small table of MSS values. It then discards all state. When the client's ACK arrives carrying that sequence number plus one, the server recomputes the hash, verifies it, and reconstructs the connection. The cost is capacity: the sequence number has only 32 bits, so options that would normally live in the SYN-queue entry, notably the window scale factor and SACK permission, cannot be fully carried, and connections established via cookies may be limited in those respects. This is why Linux enables cookies only under queue pressure rather than always.
L4.explanation: The technique is a general one worth naming: replace server-side state with a cryptographically authenticated token the client must return. The same idea underlies stateless TLS session tickets and QUIC retry tokens.

if (n > 0)                        /* got n bytes; may be FEWER than asked */

else if (errno == EAGAIN)         /* no data right now; not an error */

Setting {{c1::O_NONBLOCK}} makes recv return immediately with errno {{c2::EAGAIN}} rather than sleeping when no data is available.
A recv returning {{c3::0}} means the peer performed an orderly close, which is different from an error.
On Linux EAGAIN and EWOULDBLOCK are the {{c4::same}} value, 11.

concepts.L1: Non-blocking mode changes what a syscall does when it cannot proceed: instead of sleeping, it returns immediately with EAGAIN. This is what makes a single thread able to service many sockets, and it is a per-file-descriptor flag.
concepts.L2: EAGAIN is not an error and must never be logged as one. It is the normal, expected answer meaning nothing is ready yet, and code that treats it as failure will close healthy connections. The second trap is short writes: send() returning less than requested is normal whenever the socket buffer is nearly full.
concepts.L3: Short reads and writes follow directly from the byte-stream model. The socket send buffer here is 16384 bytes by default (net.ipv4.tcp_wmem middle value); a send() of 64 kB into a socket with 4 kB of space writes 4 kB and returns 4096, or returns EAGAIN if the buffer is entirely full. Blocking mode hides this by sleeping until it all fits, which is why blocking code looks simpler and why porting it to non-blocking exposes latent bugs everywhere a return value was ignored. The correct shape is always the same: track an offset into the buffer, loop while bytes remain, treat EAGAIN as go and wait for readiness, treat EINTR as retry immediately, and only a different errno as a real failure.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given: n = send(fd, buf, {len}, 0); if (n < 0) die(); /* assume all {len} bytes sent */. Identify every defect and give the corrected structure.
L4.answer: Two defects. First, a positive return may be less than len: send writes only what fits in the socket send buffer, so the remaining bytes are silently lost from the application's point of view, corrupting the stream. Second, n < 0 is treated as fatal, but EAGAIN on a non-blocking socket means try later and EINTR means retry now; both are normal. Correct structure: loop with an offset, send(fd, buf+off, len-off, 0); on a positive return add it to off and continue; on -1 with EAGAIN, register for writability and resume later; on -1 with EINTR, retry immediately; on any other errno, fail.
L4.explanation: Short writes are most likely under exactly the conditions you care about, a full buffer and a slow peer, so this bug hides in testing and appears under load as corrupted or truncated messages.

L4.prompt_tpl: A non-blocking socket has {avail} bytes available and the peer has not closed. Predict the return value and errno of recv(fd, buf, 4096, 0).
L4.answer: avail=0: returns -1 with errno EAGAIN (11); no data is ready and the call does not block. avail=100: returns 100; recv returns what is available, not what was asked for. avail=8192: returns 4096, filling the buffer, and the remaining 4096 bytes stay queued for the next call.
L4.explanation: recv returns the minimum of what is available and what was requested, and 0 only on orderly close. Confusing a short read with EOF is the classic bug: 0 means the peer closed, any positive value means more may follow.

                recv 2 bytes (3 left)
                epoll_wait -> STILL READY        <- level: reports state

  ET (EPOLLET): epoll_wait -> ready
                drain until recv returns EAGAIN
                epoll_wait -> NOT READY          <- edge: reports transitions

  epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd, &ev);

connection hangs forever: no further edge will arrive.

Level-triggered epoll reports a file descriptor ready whenever data is {{c1::present}}, so a partial read leaves it ready.
Edge-triggered reports only {{c2::transitions}}, so a single event covers everything that arrived.
With EPOLLET you must read until recv returns {{c3::EAGAIN}}, or the connection stalls permanently.
Edge-triggered mode is chosen to avoid {{c4::redundant}} wakeups when many descriptors are registered, not because it is faster per event.

concepts.L1: epoll reports which of many registered descriptors are ready. Level-triggered answers whether data is available now; edge-triggered answers whether new data arrived since the last report. The difference dictates how you must write the read loop.
concepts.L2: Edge-triggered is not simply faster. It removes repeated wakeups for a descriptor you have not fully drained, which matters at high descriptor counts, and it makes forgetting to drain a permanent hang rather than a busy loop. Level-triggered fails safely; edge-triggered fails silently.
concepts.L3: Trace the hang. A connection delivers 5 bytes. Under EPOLLET epoll_wait reports it once. The handler reads 2 bytes and returns, assuming it will be told again. No further data arrives, so there is no new transition, so no further event is generated, and the remaining 3 bytes sit in the receive buffer indefinitely while the connection appears idle. Under level-triggered the next epoll_wait reports it again immediately, at the cost of one extra wakeup. Measured in the sandbox: after a partial read LT reported ready again, ET did not. The rule is mechanical: under EPOLLET every handler loops until EAGAIN, accept included, or pending work is stranded.

L4.prompt_tpl: A server registers sockets with EPOLLIN | EPOLLET and its handler calls recv once for up to {size} bytes per event. Describe the failure and why it is intermittent.
L4.answer: Any time more than the read size arrives before the handler runs, the remainder is left in the receive buffer. Edge-triggered mode only signals on new arrivals, so if the peer sends nothing further there is no transition and no event, and the connection hangs with unread data indefinitely. It is intermittent because it requires a single event to carry more bytes than the read size, which depends on segment coalescing, load and timing; light testing sends small messages that fit in one read, so it passes. Fix: loop recv until it returns -1 with EAGAIN, or use level-triggered mode.
L4.explanation: The signature is a small number of connections stuck with data queued while the process looks idle, and it worsens with load because coalescing worsens with load. ss will show a non-zero Recv-Q on the stuck sockets.

L4.prompt_tpl: Choose level-triggered or edge-triggered for a server holding {n} concurrent connections, and justify by naming the cost each mode imposes.
L4.answer: At 100 connections choose level-triggered: the redundant wakeups it produces are negligible at that scale, and it fails safely because a partial read simply produces another event rather than a hang. At 100000 connections edge-triggered is worth the discipline: level-triggered re-reports every descriptor that still holds data on every epoll_wait, so a set of slow consumers produces repeated wakeups proportional to their number, and the syscall returns large ready lists that must be walked. The cost of edge-triggered is that every handler must be written to drain to EAGAIN, including accept, and any omission is a permanent stall.
L4.explanation: The tradeoff is correctness effort against wakeup volume. Most services never reach the scale where edge-triggered pays, which is why level-triggered is the default and why frameworks that expose only LT are rarely the bottleneck.

L0.cloze:
SO_REUSEPORT lets several independent sockets {{c1::bind}} the same address and port, with the kernel hashing each incoming {{c2::4-tuple}} to exactly one of them.
It replaces a shared listening descriptor and removes both the {{c3::thundering herd}} and the contention on one accept queue.
Its hazard is that adding or removing a listener {{c4::rehashes}} the set, stranding connections already queued on a departing socket.
It differs from SO_REUSEADDR, which only allows rebinding a port in {{c5::TIME_WAIT}}.

concepts.L1: A socket option allowing multiple sockets, typically one per worker process, to bind the same address and port. The kernel distributes incoming connections across them by hashing the connection's 4-tuple.
concepts.L2: SO_REUSEPORT is not a load balancer. It hashes the 4-tuple, so distribution is uniform over connections, not over work: one worker can receive all the long-lived expensive connections while another receives short ones. It also does not rebalance when a worker is busy.
concepts.L3: The rehash hazard is what bites during a rolling restart. Suppose four workers share a port and worker 3 exits. Connections whose 4-tuple hashed to worker 3 and were sitting in its accept queue, fully established but not yet accepted, are discarded when the socket closes; the client sees a reset on a connection it believes succeeded. The correct sequence is to remove the socket from the balancing set first, drain the accept queue, then close. Linux 4.5 added SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_EBPF, a BPF selection function replacing the default hash, which lets you steer around a departing worker deliberately.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team wants to scale accept throughput across {n} worker processes. Compare a single shared listening descriptor against SO_REUSEPORT, naming the specific cost of each.
L4.answer: Shared descriptor: all workers block in accept on one socket, so every arriving connection wakes contenders for one accept queue and one lock. Linux mitigates the classic thundering herd for accept by waking one waiter, but the single queue remains a contention point and load skews toward whichever worker is scheduled first. SO_REUSEPORT: each worker has its own listening socket and accept queue, and the kernel hashes the 4-tuple to pick one, so there is no shared lock and no herd. Its cost is that the hash is oblivious to load, so a worker can be handed a disproportionate share of expensive connections, and closing a listener strands its queued connections.
L4.explanation: At 4 workers the shared descriptor is usually fine; at 32 the single accept queue is measurable. The decision is about lock contention, not about fairness, since SO_REUSEPORT is worse at fairness.

L4.prompt_tpl: During a rolling restart, workers using SO_REUSEPORT are stopped with {sig} and clients report resets on connections that appeared to succeed. Explain and give the correct shutdown sequence.
L4.answer: When a listening socket closes, connections already established and sitting in that socket's accept queue are destroyed and reset, even though the client completed its handshake and considers the connection open. The kernel also rehashes the remaining listeners, so the mapping changes mid-restart. Correct sequence: remove the worker from the reuseport group first, for example by using SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_EBPF to steer new connections away or by closing the listening socket only after the group has been reconfigured; then accept and serve everything already queued; then close remaining connections gracefully; then exit.
L4.explanation: The general rule for any queue-behind-a-listener design: stop admission before you destroy the queue. The reset is invisible on the server, which is why this shows up as unexplained client-side errors during deploys.

prereqs: socket, bind, listen, accept, and the two queues

L0.cloze:
A naive file-to-socket transfer performs {{c1::4}} copies; sendfile removes the copy into and out of the {{c2::user}} buffer.
{{c3::splice}} moves data between two descriptors through a pipe with no userspace copy at all.
{{c4::io_uring}} attacks a different cost, the syscall per operation, by submitting and completing work through shared ring buffers.
{{c5::DPDK}} goes furthest, removing the kernel from the datapath and polling the NIC from userspace on dedicated cores.

concepts.L1: Three separate overheads get attacked separately: copying bytes, crossing the syscall boundary, and traversing the kernel network stack at all. sendfile and splice remove copies, io_uring removes syscalls, DPDK removes the stack.
concepts.L2: Zero-copy is not free and is often not a win. sendfile cannot transform the data, so it is useless if you compress or encrypt in userspace, and it moves the cost to page-cache pressure. Measure which of the three overheads dominates before choosing; for most services it is none of them.
concepts.L3: The name misleads. Ordinary sendfile is not zero copies: it removes the two through the user buffer, leaving disk to page cache and page cache to NIC, and the second vanishes only with scatter-gather DMA. What it reliably removes is the syscall pair and the user buffer, which is why static file servers gain and application servers do not. DPDK trades the other way: the kernel is bypassed, a core spins polling the NIC so there are no interrupts, and per-packet cost falls to tens of nanoseconds. The price is a core at 100 percent CPU regardless of traffic, no kernel firewall, no tcpdump, no ss, and a stack you now maintain. Right for a load balancer at line rate; wrong elsewhere.

L4.prompt_tpl: Choose between sendfile, splice, io_uring and plain read/write for {workload}, and name the dominant cost each choice addresses.

workload: serving static files over plain HTTP
a proxy forwarding socket to socket
a service handling 500k small requests per second

L4.answer: Static files over plain HTTP: sendfile, because the data is untransformed and the copies through userspace are pure overhead. TLS dynamic responses: plain read/write, because encryption requires touching the bytes; sendfile applies only with kernel TLS offload, and dynamic content is not in the page cache anyway. Socket-to-socket proxy: splice, since it moves pages between two descriptors through a pipe with no userspace copy and the proxy does not inspect the data. 500k small requests per second: io_uring, because the dominant cost there is the syscall per operation, not the byte copies, and batched submission with multishot accept removes most of them.
L4.explanation: Match the tool to the dominant cost. Copy overhead scales with bytes, syscall overhead scales with operations. A small-request workload has few bytes and many operations, so copy elimination buys nothing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team proposes DPDK for their {service} to reduce latency. List what they lose and state the condition under which it is justified.
L4.answer: They lose the entire kernel datapath and everything built on it: iptables and nftables filtering, conntrack, tcpdump, ss and the /proc counters, kernel TCP with its congestion control and offloads, and the ability to run anything else on the polling cores, which burn 100 percent CPU regardless of load. They also take on maintaining a userspace TCP stack. It is justified only when the service is packet-rate bound at or near line rate on a dedicated machine and the per-packet kernel cost has been measured as the bottleneck, which is plausible for an L4 load balancer and implausible for an API gateway or an internal RPC service whose time goes to application work.
L4.explanation: The honest test: profile first. If kernel network processing is not a double-digit share of CPU, kernel bypass cannot help, and XDP or io_uring will get most of the benefit while keeping the observability tools.

sections.note: Latency has a floor set by physics. Bandwidth is a purchase; round trips are a negotiation with the speed of light.

concepts.t: The speed of light in fibre is the floor

L0.body:
c = 299792458 m/s in vacuum. Single-mode fibre has refractive index n ~ 1.4675.

  v = c / n = 299792458 / 1.4675 = 204287876 m/s = 204288 km/s

  one-way per km = 1 / 204288 s = 4.895 us
  RTT      per km = 9.790 us          -> a useful rule: ~10 us of RTT per km

  1000 km  ->  9.79 ms RTT   (floor, straight line, no equipment)
  5570 km  -> 54.53 ms RTT   (New York to London, great circle)

Real paths are 1.3x to 1.5x the great circle, plus switching and
serialisation. Nothing you buy makes this smaller.
L0.cloze:
Light in single-mode fibre travels at $c/n$ with $n \approx 1.4675$, giving about {{c1::204288}} km/s, roughly two thirds of $c$.
That is about {{c2::10}} microseconds of round-trip time per kilometre.
Real fibre routes are typically {{c3::1.3 to 1.5}} times the great-circle distance because cables follow terrain and existing rights of way.
This floor is unaffected by {{c4::bandwidth}}: buying a fatter link changes throughput and not one microsecond of propagation delay.

concepts.L1: Propagation delay is set by the refractive index of glass. At $n \approx 1.4675$ signals travel at about 204288 km/s, which fixes a hard lower bound of roughly 10 microseconds of round-trip time per kilometre of path.
concepts.L2: The floor applies to the route, not the map distance. Cables follow coastlines, rights of way and existing conduit, so a 1.3 to 1.5 multiplier on the great circle is normal and the measured RTT sits above the geometric floor by that factor plus equipment delay.
concepts.L3: Derive it rather than memorising the number. The phase velocity in a medium is $v = c/n$. For single-mode silica fibre at 1550 nm, $n \approx 1.4675$, so $v = 299792458/1.4675 = 2.0429 \times 10^{8}$ m/s, about 68 percent of $c$. One kilometre one way is $1000/2.0429\times10^{8} = 4.895\,\mu$s, so a round trip is $9.79\,\mu$s. New York to London is 5570 km on the great circle, giving a floor of 54.5 ms; the best-engineered transatlantic routes measure about 59 ms, which is close to the geometric limit and is why they were worth building. A commodity path measures 70 to 76 ms, a 1.3 to 1.4 route multiplier. No engineering improves this number.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute the round-trip propagation floor in fibre for a great-circle distance of {km} km, and the expected real-world RTT at a route multiplier of 1.4. Answer with the real-world RTT in milliseconds at the 1.4 route multiplier.
L4.answer: RTT_floor = 2*km/204288 s = km * 9.790 us. 5570 km -> 54.53 ms floor, 76.4 ms at 1.4x. 13582 km (San Francisco to Singapore) -> 132.97 ms, 186.2 ms. 16994 km (London to Sydney) -> 166.37 ms, 232.9 ms. 4129 km (New York to San Francisco) -> 40.42 ms, 56.6 ms.
L4.explanation: The 1.4 multiplier is empirical and matches measured inter-region latencies closely. Use the floor to decide whether a latency target is achievable at all; if the target is below the floor, no engineering will reach it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive the propagation velocity in fibre from $c$ and a refractive index of {n}, then derive the round-trip microseconds per kilometre. Answer with the round-trip microseconds per kilometre.
L4.answer: v = c/n. n=1.4675: v = 204288 km/s, RTT per km = 2000/204288 s per km... in microseconds, 2*1e6/204288 = 9.790 us/km. n=1.5: v = 199862 km/s, 10.007 us/km. n=1.46: v = 205337 km/s, 9.740 us/km. The answer is insensitive to the exact index, which is why 10 us/km is a safe working rule.
L4.explanation: The whole range of plausible indices gives 9.7 to 10.0 microseconds per kilometre, so the round number is accurate to within 3 percent. Memorise 10 us/km of RTT and you can sanity-check any latency claim in your head.

concepts.t: What a cross-region round trip actually costs

L0.body:
Great circle, fibre floor, and the realistic figure at a 1.4x route multiplier:

  route                       km      floor RTT   realistic
  Ashburn - Dublin          5461      53.5 ms      74.8 ms
  New York - London         5570      54.5 ms      76.4 ms
  New York - San Francisco  4129      40.4 ms      56.6 ms
  San Francisco - Tokyo     8275      81.0 ms     113.4 ms
  San Francisco - Singapore 13582    133.0 ms     186.2 ms
  London - Sydney          16994     166.4 ms     232.9 ms

12 sequential queries Ashburn to Dublin: 12 x 74.8 = 898 ms of waiting.
L0.cloze:
A round trip between the US east coast and Ireland costs about {{c1::75}} ms, of which roughly 53 ms is pure physics.
The cost of a chatty protocol is the number of {{c2::sequential}} round trips multiplied by that figure, so 12 dependent queries cost about 0.9 s.
London to Sydney is about {{c3::233}} ms, meaning fewer than five sequential round trips fit in one second.
The fix is never a faster link; it is fewer {{c4::round trips}}, achieved by batching, pipelining, or moving computation next to the data.

concepts.L1: The practical latency table. Inter-region round trips run from about 55 ms within a continent to over 230 ms antipodally, and every dependent request in a chain pays the full amount again.
concepts.L2: Latency budgets are consumed by dependency, not by volume. Twelve queries issued in parallel cost one round trip; the same twelve issued sequentially cost twelve. Almost every slow cross-region page is a dependency chain, and the fix is restructuring the chain, not the network.
concepts.L3: Work an example end to end. A service in Ashburn reads from a database in Dublin, 74.8 ms round trip. Rendering a page needs 12 queries where each depends on the previous result: $12 \times 74.8 = 898$ ms of pure waiting, with zero compute. Restructure so the 12 become 3 batches of independent queries and the cost falls to $3 \times 74.8 = 224$ ms, a 4x improvement with no infrastructure change. Move the service to Dublin and the same 12 sequential queries over a 0.5 ms local network cost 6 ms, a 150x improvement. That ordering is the lesson: cut round trips first, since it is a code change; then colocate; only then look at the network, which cannot go below the fibre floor.

L4.prompt_tpl: A page issues {n} database queries, each depending on the previous result, from a service {ms} ms away from the database. Compute total latency, and the latency if the queries can be reduced to 3 dependent batches. Answer with the sequential total in milliseconds.
L4.answer: Sequential total = n * ms. Batched = 3 * ms. n=12, ms=74.8: 897.6 ms sequential, 224.4 ms batched. n=20, ms=74.8: 1496 ms vs 224.4 ms. n=6, ms=232.9: 1397.4 ms vs 698.7 ms. n=12, ms=0.5: 6 ms vs 1.5 ms.
L4.explanation: The saving is a ratio of round-trip counts, n/3, and is entirely independent of bandwidth and of how much data each query returns. This is why batching is the highest-leverage change available on a cross-region path.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team wants to cut the {ms} ms cross-region round trip their service depends on. Rank the available interventions and state which are bounded by physics.
L4.answer: First, reduce the number of dependent round trips by batching, pipelining or denormalising: this is a code change, has no floor, and typically yields the largest factor. Second, colocate the service with the data, which replaces a cross-region round trip with a sub-millisecond one and is the largest single improvement available. Third, add a read replica or cache in the local region, which trades consistency for latency. Fourth, buy a better-engineered path: this is bounded by the fibre floor, roughly 53 ms of the 74.8, 133 of the 186.2, and 166 of the 232.9, so the ceiling on this intervention is small. Buying more bandwidth does nothing at all.
L4.explanation: Compute the floor before evaluating any proposal. If a vendor promises a cross-region round trip below the great-circle fibre floor, they are either wrong or routing through somewhere you did not expect.

prereqs: The speed of light in fibre is the floor

sections.note: This is where multi-node training actually fails. Everything above was preparation for this section and the next.

L0.body:
A k-ary fat-tree (Al-Fares, Loukissas, Vahdat, SIGCOMM 2008) built only from
identical k-port switches:

  hosts        = k^3 / 4
  pods         = k          each with k/2 edge and k/2 aggregation switches
  core         = (k/2)^2 = k^2/4
  switches     = 5k^2/4

  k = 48:  hosts = 27648   pods = 48   core = 576   switches = 2880
  k = 64:  hosts = 65536   pods = 64   core = 1024  switches = 5120

Every host pair has (k/2)^2 equal-cost paths. The topology is built for
BISECTION, not for hop count: any host can reach any other at full line rate
if traffic is spread across those paths.
L0.cloze:
A $k$-ary fat-tree supports {{c1::$k^{3}/4$}} hosts using only identical $k$-port switches.
It has $k$ {{c2::pods}}, each with $k/2$ edge and $k/2$ aggregation switches, and $k^{2}/4$ core switches.
Between any pair of hosts in different pods there are {{c3::$(k/2)^{2}$}} equal-cost paths.
For $k=48$ the design carries {{c4::27648}} hosts with 2880 switches.
Its point is uniform {{c5::bisection bandwidth}}, not short paths.

concepts.L1: A multi-rooted tree built entirely from identical commodity switches, arranged so that aggregate capacity does not narrow as you climb. Its purpose is that any permutation of host-to-host traffic can run at line rate.
concepts.L2: The fat-tree is not about reducing hops; every inter-pod path is exactly six hops. It is about removing the assumption that traffic is local. Classic tree topologies assumed most traffic stayed within a rack, which is false for training, where an all-reduce touches every node.
concepts.L3: Count the switches to see why commodity parts win. A $k$-ary fat-tree uses $k/2$ edge and $k/2$ aggregation switches in each of $k$ pods, plus $(k/2)^{2}$ core: $k^{2} + k^{2}/4 = 5k^{2}/4$. For $k=48$ that is 2880 identical 48-port switches serving 27648 hosts. The alternative, a two-level tree with a giant chassis switch at the root, needs one device with 27648 ports, which does not exist and would be a single failure domain if it did. The fat-tree trades one impossible switch for 2880 ordinary ones, with incremental failure and upgrade as a bonus. The cost is that all those equal-cost paths must actually be used, which is ECMP's job and where it goes wrong.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a k-ary fat-tree with k = {k}, compute the number of hosts, the number of core switches, the total switch count, and the number of equal-cost paths between hosts in different pods. Answer with the number of hosts.
L4.explanation: Note that the core switch count and the path count are the same number, k^2/4: each core switch is the top of exactly one distinct path. That identity is the cleanest way to remember the structure.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive why a fat-tree needs $5k^{{2}}/4$ switches to serve $k^{{3}}/4$ hosts, and explain what this buys over a single {alt} switch.
L4.answer: Each pod holds k/2 edge switches, each with k/2 ports facing hosts and k/2 facing aggregation, giving (k/2)*(k/2) = k^2/4 hosts per pod. With k pods that is k^3/4 hosts. Switch count: k pods times (k/2 edge + k/2 aggregation) = k^2 switches, plus (k/2)^2 = k^2/4 core, totalling 5k^2/4. Against a single large switch it buys three things: the parts are commodity k-port devices that exist and are cheap, failure of any one removes a fraction of capacity rather than everything, and capacity can be added a pod at a time. The cost is complexity: many equal-cost paths that must be balanced across, and a control plane to manage them.
L4.explanation: The per-pod host count k^2/4 is the step people miss: half of each edge switch's ports face up, not down, which is exactly what makes the tree non-blocking.

prereqs: Longest-prefix match and the forwarding table

L0.body:
Cut the network into two equal halves the worst way you can; bisection
bandwidth is the capacity crossing that cut.

  Full bisection, N hosts at R: bisection = (N/2)*R
    1024 x 400 Gb/s -> 204.8 Tb/s = 25.6 TB/s
    4096 x 400 Gb/s -> 819.2 Tb/s = 102.4 TB/s

Oversubscription at a leaf = downlink capacity / uplink capacity:
  48 x 25G down = 1200G ; 8 x 100G up  =   800G -> 1.5:1
  32 x 200G     = 6400G ; 8 x 400G up  =  3200G -> 2:1
  32 x 400G     =12800G ; 16 x 800G up = 12800G -> 1:1

At 2:1 a rack-crossing all-reduce runs at HALF the intra-rack rate,
with no error reported anywhere.
L0.cloze:
Bisection bandwidth is the capacity crossing the {{c1::worst-case}} cut of the network into two equal halves.
A non-blocking fabric of $N$ hosts at rate $R$ has bisection {{c2::$NR/2$}}.
Oversubscription at a leaf is downlink capacity divided by {{c3::uplink}} capacity; 48 ports of 25G over 8 ports of 100G is {{c4::1.5}}:1.
A job whose traffic crosses racks runs at the {{c5::oversubscription ratio}} of its worst leaf, not at link rate.

concepts.L1: Bisection bandwidth measures the fabric's ability to carry all-to-all traffic; oversubscription measures how much capacity was removed to save money. Both are properties of the topology, not of any link.
concepts.L2: Oversubscription is invisible until the traffic pattern changes. A fabric at 4:1 serves web traffic perfectly, because that traffic is mostly north-south and rack-local. The same fabric halves and halves again the throughput of a distributed training job, which is all-to-all by construction, and nothing reports an error.
concepts.L3: Compute what oversubscription costs a collective. Take 32 nodes with 400 Gb/s NICs across four racks at 2:1 per leaf. Inside a rack, nodes exchange at 50 GB/s. A ring crossing rack boundaries has every inter-rack hop limited to half the uplink share, and the slowest link paces the whole ring, so the collective runs at 25 GB/s. The measured bus bandwidth is therefore half what a single-rack test showed, and the job merely appears to scale badly. Hence training clusters are built 1:1 to the leaf, and hence NCCL's topology detection matters: it keeps rings inside high-bandwidth domains when it can see them.

L4.prompt_tpl: A leaf switch has {nd} downlinks at {dr} Gb/s and {nu} uplinks at {ur} Gb/s. Compute the oversubscription ratio and the effective per-node bandwidth for a job whose traffic all leaves the rack. Answer with the oversubscription ratio.
L4.answer: ratio = (nd*dr)/(nu*ur); effective per-node = dr/ratio when all nodes send off-rack simultaneously. 48x25 over 8x100: 1200/800 = 1.5:1, effective 16.7 Gb/s per node. 32x200 over 8x400: 6400/3200 = 2:1, effective 100 Gb/s. 64x100 over 16x400: 6400/6400 = 1:1, effective 100 Gb/s. 32x200 over 16x800: 6400/12800 = 0.5:1, so uplinks exceed downlinks and the leaf is non-blocking with headroom.
L4.explanation: The effective figure assumes every node sends off-rack at once, which is exactly what a collective does. For web traffic the same ratio is harmless because only a fraction of nodes are sending north at any instant.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute the full-bisection bandwidth of a fabric with {n} hosts each attached at {r} Gb/s, in Tb/s and in TB/s. Answer with the bisection bandwidth in Gb/s.
L4.explanation: The half is the whole subtlety: in the worst-case cut only half the hosts are on each side, so only half the NICs can be sending across it. Quoting N*R instead of N*R/2 is the most common error in fabric sizing.

L0.body:
ECMP hashes the 5-tuple to pick one of N equal-cost next hops:

  h = hash(src_ip, dst_ip, sport, dport, proto) mod N

Per-FLOW, not per-packet, so TCP never sees reordering. That choice is
the whole problem: a flow is pinned to one path for its lifetime.

  8 large flows over 8 paths, hash uniform:
    P(no two collide) = 8!/8^8 = 0.0024
    expected empty paths = 8*(7/8)^8 = 2.75

So on average about a third of the paths carry nothing while others carry
two or three elephant flows, and each collided flow runs at half rate.
L0.cloze:
ECMP selects a next hop by hashing the {{c1::5-tuple}}, so all packets of one flow take one path and TCP never sees reordering.
The cost is that a flow is {{c2::pinned}} for its lifetime, and two elephants that hash to the same link each get half of it.
With 8 flows over 8 paths the probability of no collision is $8!/8^{8} = $ {{c3::0.0024}}, and about {{c4::2.75}} paths are expected to carry nothing.
The standard mitigations are more, smaller flows, or {{c5::flowlet}} switching, which rebalances at natural gaps in a flow.

concepts.L1: Equal-cost multipath spreads traffic over the many paths a Clos fabric provides by hashing each flow's 5-tuple. The hash is per flow so that packets within a flow stay ordered.
concepts.L2: ECMP is a randomised balancer, not a balancer. With few large flows it behaves like balls into bins, and collisions are the common case: eight flows over eight paths collide with probability 0.9976. Adding paths does not fix it; adding flows does.
concepts.L3: The arithmetic is the birthday problem: with $f$ flows over $p$ paths, $P(\text{no collision}) = p!/((p-f)!\,p^{f})$ and the expected idle-path count is $p(1-1/p)^{f}$. For $f=p=8$ that is 0.0024 and 2.75, so a topology engineered for full bisection delivers well under it for a handful of elephants, and the shortfall is invisible in every utilisation graph because collided links look healthy at 100 percent. Three fixes: many smaller flows so the law of large numbers applies, which is why NCCL opens multiple channels; flowlet switching, rehashing at gaps longer than the path delay difference; or per-packet spraying with a reordering-tolerant transport, as InfiniBand adaptive routing does.

L4.prompt_tpl: With {f} equal-sized elephant flows hashed uniformly over {p} ECMP paths, compute the probability that no two flows collide and the expected number of idle paths. Answer with the expected number of idle paths.
L4.explanation: The probability of a clean assignment collapses quickly once f approaches p, which is exactly the regime a training job creates: one big flow per peer, and as many peers as ranks. This is why per-flow ECMP fails on collectives specifically.

L4.prompt_tpl: A training job achieves {frac} of expected all-reduce bandwidth on a non-oversubscribed fabric, and link utilisation graphs look healthy. Diagnose and rank the fixes.
L4.answer: ECMP flow collisions. A collective creates few large long-lived flows; two hashing to one link each get half of it while other equal-cost links sit idle. Utilisation graphs look healthy because the collided link genuinely is at 100 percent. Fixes, ranked: increase the number of flows so the hash averages out, which for NCCL means raising NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS or letting it use more channels; enable flowlet-based load balancing or adaptive routing on the fabric if the switches support it; use per-packet spraying with a reordering-tolerant transport, as InfiniBand adaptive routing and modern AI Ethernet fabrics do; as a last resort, vary source ports to reshuffle the hash, which is a lottery rather than a fix.
L4.explanation: The diagnostic tell is high bandwidth variance between otherwise identical runs: the same job reshuffles ports each time and draws a different assignment. A collective whose throughput changes materially between identical runs is almost always hash collisions.

L0.body:
RDMA writes into a remote process's memory with no CPU on the far side.

  Queue Pair = send queue + receive queue; a Completion Queue reports
  finished work. Memory must be REGISTERED (pinned, rkey issued)
  before the NIC may touch it.

  two-sided: ibv_post_send(SEND) -> remote must have posted a RECV
  one-sided: ibv_post_send(RDMA_WRITE|READ, remote addr + rkey)
             -> remote CPU is NOT involved and is never notified

  Transports: RC (reliable connected), UC, UD (unreliable datagram).

Latency: ~1-2 us for a one-sided READ vs ~10-50 us for a kernel TCP RPC.
L0.cloze:
An RDMA connection is a {{c1::queue pair}}, and completions are reported through a completion queue polled by the application.
Buffers must be {{c2::registered}}, meaning pinned and given an rkey, before the NIC may access them.
A {{c3::one-sided}} operation (RDMA WRITE or READ) completes without involving the remote CPU at all.
{{c4::RC}} is the reliable connected transport; UD is unreliable datagram and scales better because it needs one queue pair per process rather than per peer.

concepts.L1: A network interface that writes directly into a remote process's registered memory, bypassing both kernels. The application posts work requests to a queue pair and polls a completion queue; the NIC does the transfer.
concepts.L2: The saving is not the copy, it is the CPU and the interrupt. One-sided operations complete with no remote CPU involvement, so the receiver cannot apply logic, validate, or even know the write happened unless the sender tells it separately. Every RDMA protocol needs its own completion signalling.
concepts.L3: Memory registration is where RDMA leaks into your design. Registration pins pages so they cannot be swapped or moved and issues an rkey the remote side presents. It costs tens of microseconds and consumes a NIC translation-table entry, so registering per operation destroys the latency advantage. Real systems register large buffers once at startup and manage them as an arena. Second, scale: reliable connected transport needs a queue pair per peer, so $n$ fully connected processes need $O(n^{2})$ of them, and NIC cache misses on QP state degrade badly past a few hundred. That is why some designs use unreliable datagram with application-level reliability instead.

L4.prompt_tpl: Choose one-sided RDMA WRITE or two-sided SEND for {usecase}, and state the completion-signalling problem your choice creates.
L4.answer: Key-value GET: one-sided READ if the client can locate the value itself, since it removes the server CPU from the path entirely and gives 1 to 2 microsecond latency; the problem is that the client must know the address, so the index must be replicated or read first, often costing a second round trip. RPC with server-side logic: two-sided SEND, because the server must execute code, and one-sided operations give it no notification at all. Gradient exchange: one-sided WRITE into pre-registered receive buffers, because the destination is known in advance and the receiver only needs to know when the write completed, which is signalled separately with a flag write or a completion-queue event.
L4.explanation: The rule: one-sided is right when the sender already knows where the bytes go and the receiver needs no logic. Otherwise you will rebuild notification on top of it, and two-sided already has it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service calls ibv_reg_mr per request for a {size} buffer and reports RDMA latency worse than TCP. Explain and give the fix.
L4.answer: Memory registration is a slow control-plane operation, tens of microseconds, because it pins the pages, walks the page tables and installs a translation entry in the NIC. Doing it per request puts an operation an order of magnitude more expensive than the transfer itself on the critical path, so the measured latency is dominated by registration and RDMA loses to TCP. It also exhausts the NIC's translation cache, degrading everything else. Fix: register a large arena once at startup and allocate request buffers from it, so the data path only posts work requests; if buffers must be dynamic, keep a pool of pre-registered buffers and recycle them.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common RDMA performance bug. The mental model to keep: registration is like mmap, not like malloc. It belongs at startup, never in a request handler.

L0.body:
InfiniBand         RoCEv2
  wire       its own L1/L2      Ethernet+IP+UDP (port 4791)
  loss       credit-based,      Ethernet drops by default;
             lossless by design needs PFC to be lossless
  congestion in the fabric      DCQCN, bolted on with ECN
  switches   IB only            standard Ethernet
  4x port    NDR 400, XDR 800   400 and 800 GbE

InfiniBand is lossless because link-level CREDITS mean a sender never
transmits without buffer space at the receiver. Ethernet has no such
mechanism, so RoCE simulates it with PAUSE frames -- and that is where
the trouble starts.
L0.cloze:
RoCEv2 encapsulates RDMA in {{c1::UDP}} (port 4791) over IP, so it is routable across a standard Ethernet fabric.
InfiniBand is lossless by construction, using link-level {{c2::credits}} so a sender never transmits without buffer space at the receiver.
Ethernet drops by default, so RoCEv2 must simulate losslessness with {{c3::PFC}} pause frames.
Congestion control is inside the fabric for InfiniBand and is {{c4::DCQCN}}, layered on ECN, for RoCEv2.

concepts.L1: Two ways to carry RDMA. InfiniBand is a purpose-built lossless fabric with its own physical and link layers; RoCEv2 puts the same RDMA verbs into UDP over ordinary routable Ethernet.
concepts.L2: RoCEv2 is not simply InfiniBand on cheaper switches. Its reliability model assumes a lossless link, which Ethernet does not provide, so losslessness must be manufactured with priority flow control. Every operational hazard in a RoCE deployment traces back to that substitution.
concepts.L3: The credit mechanism is the real difference. A receiver grants buffer credits and the sender transmits only while it holds them, so a buffer cannot overflow and the fabric never drops for congestion; losslessness is a property of the link protocol. RoCEv2 has no such protocol, so it uses PFC: a switch ingress buffer crossing a threshold sends a PAUSE frame upstream, halting that traffic class. That is blunt, per-hop, per-class backpressure with no notion of which flow caused the problem, so it pauses innocent flows, propagates congestion backwards, and can form cycles. So every serious RoCE deployment also runs DCQCN: PFC is an emergency brake that should almost never fire.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team is choosing between InfiniBand and RoCEv2 for a {n}-GPU training cluster. Give the honest tradeoff on both sides.
L4.answer: InfiniBand: losslessness is structural rather than configured, congestion control and adaptive routing are in the fabric, and the operational failure modes are well understood; the costs are a single vendor, a separate management plane, and staff who must learn a second network technology. RoCEv2: standard Ethernet switches, one network to operate, routable and familiar tooling; the cost is that losslessness must be configured correctly across every switch with PFC and DCQCN, and misconfiguration produces pause storms and potential deadlock rather than graceful degradation. At 64 GPUs either works and RoCEv2's operational simplicity usually wins. At 1024 and above the configuration burden is real either way, and the deciding factors are usually existing staff expertise and vendor relationships, not the protocols.
L4.explanation: The honest summary: InfiniBand moves complexity into the fabric you buy, RoCEv2 moves it into the configuration you own. Neither removes it. Read Guo et al., RDMA over Commodity Ethernet at Scale, before choosing RoCE.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why RoCEv2 needs priority flow control while InfiniBand does not, in terms of what each link layer guarantees.
L4.answer: RDMA's reliable transport was designed assuming the link never drops packets for congestion, so its loss recovery is minimal; on the original InfiniBand link layer this holds because of credit-based flow control, where a sender may transmit only while the receiver has granted buffer credits, making overflow impossible. Ethernet has no credit mechanism and drops when a buffer fills, so RoCEv2 running RDMA transport over Ethernet would suffer frequent, expensive go-back-N recovery. PFC manufactures the missing guarantee by having a switch send PAUSE frames upstream for a traffic class when its ingress buffer crosses a threshold, stopping the sender before overflow.
L4.explanation: The key asymmetry: credits are per-link and per-connection and prevent overflow before it can happen; PAUSE is per-link and per-class and reacts after a threshold, halting everything in the class. That coarseness is the source of every PFC pathology.

concepts.t: PFC, and the deadlock it can cause

L0.body:
PFC (802.1Qbb) pauses ONE of 8 traffic classes on ONE link:

  class 3 ingress buffer crosses XOFF -> PAUSE(class 3, quanta)
  upstream port stops class 3 until XON or timer expiry

Two failure modes, by severity:

  1. Pause propagation. Congestion at one port backs up hop by hop,
     throttling flows that never touched it.

  2. DEADLOCK. PAUSE creates a buffer dependency A->B. If routing makes
     those cyclic -- a link flap plus rerouting can do this even in a
     Clos that is acyclic when healthy -- no port drains and the class
     stops forever. Only a manual reset clears it.
L0.cloze:
PFC pauses a single {{c1::traffic class}} on a single link, using PAUSE frames sent upstream when an ingress buffer crosses a threshold.
Its milder failure is pause {{c2::propagation}}, in which congestion at one port backs up hop by hop and throttles unrelated flows.
Its severe failure is {{c3::deadlock}}, which occurs when the buffer dependencies PAUSE creates form a {{c4::cycle}}.
A Clos fabric is acyclic when healthy, but a link failure plus rerouting can create the cycle, which is why deadlock appears during incidents rather than in testing.

concepts.L1: Priority flow control is a per-link, per-class stop signal that lets Ethernet emulate a lossless fabric. It works by pausing an upstream port rather than by dropping, which converts a drop problem into a blocking problem.
concepts.L2: PFC deadlock is not hypothetical and it is not fixed by a healthy topology. Guo and colleagues documented it in production at Microsoft: an unhealthy state, typically a link down and traffic rerouted up-down-up, creates a cyclic buffer dependency in a topology that is loop-free under normal routing.
concepts.L3: Trace the cycle. Under normal Clos routing traffic goes up then down, never up again, so buffer dependencies are acyclic. Now a leaf-to-spine link fails. Traffic for a server under that leaf goes up to a spine, down to another leaf, and up again: the up-down-up pattern. With two such rerouted flows in opposite directions, port A waits on a PAUSE from B while B waits on one from A. Neither drains, the class is dead, and no timeout resolves it, because PFC's whole intent is to wait rather than drop. Mitigations: run DCQCN so ECN reacts long before PFC fires, enable a PFC watchdog that starts dropping when a port stays paused, and avoid routing that produces up-down-up.

L4.prompt_tpl: Review a proposed RoCEv2 deployment that relies on PFC alone, with no DCQCN, across {racks} racks. Enumerate the failure modes in severity order and give the mitigations.
L4.answer: Worst: PFC deadlock. A link failure plus rerouting can create up-down-up paths whose buffer dependencies form a cycle; the paused class then never drains and only a manual reset recovers it, taking down all RDMA traffic in that class fabric-wide. Next: pause propagation, where one congested victim port backs pressure up the tree and throttles flows that never touched it, so a single slow receiver degrades the whole cluster. Next: unfairness and head-of-line blocking within the paused class, since PAUSE is class-granular and cannot distinguish the offending flow. Mitigations: run DCQCN so ECN marking reduces sender rates long before buffers reach the PFC threshold; enable a PFC watchdog that detects a port paused beyond a threshold and drops rather than blocking; set ECN thresholds well below PFC thresholds; and monitor PAUSE frame counters, treating any sustained rate as an incident.
L4.explanation: The correct mental model is that PFC should almost never fire. If PAUSE frames are a normal part of steady-state operation, the deployment is one link failure away from a deadlock.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a Clos fabric that is provably loop-free during normal operation can still deadlock under PFC when {event} occurs.
L4.answer: Normal Clos routing is strictly up then down, so the buffer dependency graph is a DAG and no cycle can form. When a link fails, some destinations are no longer reachable by a pure up-down path, and the fabric reroutes: up to a spine, down to a leaf, then up again to a different spine. That up-down-up pattern breaks the level ordering that guaranteed acyclicity. With two such rerouted flows in opposing directions, port A's buffer depends on B draining while B's depends on A, and PFC makes each wait rather than drop, so neither ever drains. The deadlock is a property of the transient routing state, not of the designed topology, which is why it survives topology review and appears only during incidents.
L4.explanation: The general lesson: acyclicity arguments that rely on the healthy topology are not safety arguments. Any blocking protocol must be verified against the reroute states the control plane can actually produce.

L0.body:
DCQCN (Zhu et al., SIGCOMM 2015) keeps PFC from ever having to fire. Three roles:

  CP (switch):  mark ECN CE when queue > K_min, with probability
                rising to P_max at K_max
  NP (rx NIC):  on seeing CE, return a Congestion Notification
                Packet (CNP)
  RP (tx NIC):  on CNP, cut rate multiplicatively; with no CNP,
                recover additively -- ALL IN NIC HARDWARE

  Thresholds must satisfy:  K_min < K_max << PFC XOFF threshold

so rates fall long before any buffer reaches the pause threshold. Set
ECN thresholds above PFC's and DCQCN is dead code.
L0.cloze:
DCQCN marks {{c1::ECN}} at the switch, has the receiving NIC return a {{c2::CNP}}, and has the sending NIC adjust its rate, all in hardware.
Its purpose is to keep queues short enough that {{c3::PFC}} never has to fire.
The ECN marking thresholds must be set well {{c4::below}} the PFC pause threshold, or the rate control never engages before the fabric starts pausing.
It runs at the {{c5::NIC}} rather than in the kernel because RDMA bypasses the kernel entirely.

concepts.L1: The rate-based congestion control for RoCEv2. Switches mark ECN, receiving NICs return congestion notification packets, and sending NICs adjust rate in hardware, so queues stay short and PFC stays idle.
concepts.L2: DCQCN is not optional decoration on a PFC deployment; it is the thing that makes PFC survivable. And the ordering of thresholds is the entire configuration: set ECN marking above the PFC pause threshold and DCQCN is dead code, because pausing happens first every time.
concepts.L3: Why hardware follows from where RDMA lives. DCTCP does this job for TCP in the kernel, adjusting cwnd on marked ACKs. RDMA has no kernel in the datapath and no per-packet software at all, so the reaction point must be the NIC and the feedback an explicit packet it can generate: the CNP. It is also rate-based rather than window-based because an RDMA NIC paces from a rate register, not from a congestion window. The practical consequence is that DCQCN's parameters, $K_{\min}$, $K_{\max}$, $P_{\max}$, the rate-decrease factor and the timers, are split between switch configuration and NIC firmware, so tuning means touching two vendors' devices consistently.

L4.prompt_tpl: A RoCEv2 fabric shows a high and sustained PAUSE frame rate with DCQCN enabled, and ECN marking thresholds set at {kmin} of buffer occupancy while the PFC XOFF threshold is at {xoff}. Diagnose.
L4.answer: The threshold ordering is inverted. PFC pauses at 50 percent (or 40) occupancy, before the queue ever reaches the 80 percent (or 60) mark at which ECN would be applied, so no CE marks are generated, no CNPs are returned, and DCQCN never adjusts any sender's rate. The fabric therefore runs entirely on PFC backpressure, with all its propagation and deadlock exposure, while DCQCN appears enabled and does nothing. Fix: set K_min and K_max well below the PFC XOFF threshold, typically marking beginning at a small fraction of the buffer, so rate control engages long before pausing.
L4.explanation: The invariant to check on any RoCE fabric: K_min < K_max << XOFF. Verify it as measured occupancy, not as vendor default percentages, since switches differ in whether thresholds are per-port, per-class or shared-pool.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why DCQCN must run in NIC hardware and be rate-based, while DCTCP can run in the kernel and be window-based. Refer to a {rate} link.
L4.answer: RDMA bypasses the kernel entirely: there is no software on the datapath to inspect acknowledgements or adjust a window, so the reaction point must be the NIC and the congestion signal must be an explicit packet the NIC can generate and consume, which is the CNP. DCTCP has the kernel processing every ACK, so it can piggyback the ECN echo and adjust cwnd in software. Rate-based rather than window-based follows from the same place: an RDMA NIC transmits from a pacing rate register, and at 100 or 400 Gb/s the per-packet software work a window would require does not exist. A window also requires per-packet accounting the NIC would have to do in hardware for millions of packets per second.
L4.explanation: The general point: congestion control has to live wherever the datapath is. Move the datapath out of the kernel and every control loop attached to it must move too, which is also why QUIC's congestion control lives in userspace.
