L0.body:
Without it, a GPU-to-remote-GPU transfer stages through host memory:

  GPU0 -> host DRAM -> NIC -> wire -> NIC -> host DRAM -> GPU1
  two extra PCIe crossings, plus a CPU-mediated copy each side

With GPUDirect RDMA the NIC DMAs straight to and from GPU memory:

  GPU0 HBM -> NIC -> wire -> NIC -> GPU1

Requirements that bite:
  - NIC and GPU under one PCIe switch; across sockets the path crosses
    the inter-socket link and loses most of the gain
  - GPU BAR1 large enough to expose the buffers
  - matching driver stack (nvidia-peermem)

NCCL prints the chosen path under NCCL_DEBUG=INFO.
L0.cloze:
GPUDirect RDMA lets the NIC DMA directly into {{c1::GPU}} memory, removing the staging copy through host DRAM and two PCIe crossings.
The benefit depends on {{c2::PCIe topology}}: the NIC and GPU should sit under the same PCIe switch, since crossing sockets can erase most of the gain.
The GPU must expose its memory through a sufficiently large {{c3::BAR1}} aperture.
You confirm the path NCCL actually chose by reading the {{c4::NCCL_DEBUG=INFO}} topology output, not by assuming it is enabled.

concepts.L1: A path that lets a network adapter read and write GPU device memory directly over PCIe, removing the bounce through host memory. It is what makes multi-node GPU communication approach the wire rate.
concepts.L2: Whether it is in use is a topology question, not a software switch. A NIC on a different PCIe root complex from the GPU will still work, and will still be called GPUDirect, while the traffic crosses the inter-socket link and delivers a fraction of the bandwidth. Read the topology, do not trust the feature flag.
concepts.L3: Placement dominates because PCIe peer-to-peer under one switch never touches the CPU, while peer-to-peer across root complexes traverses the inter-socket interconnect, whose peer-to-peer performance is far worse than its memory bandwidth suggests and is sometimes disabled outright. A typical eight-GPU node pairs each GPU with a NIC under a shared switch, giving a clean 400 Gb/s per GPU. Bind the wrong NIC to a rank, easy to do with a careless NCCL_IB_HCA, and that rank crosses the socket link and drags the whole collective to its speed, since a collective runs at the pace of its slowest participant. The diagnostic is always NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and the printed topology.

L4.prompt_tpl: An 8-GPU node achieves full all-reduce bandwidth intra-node but only {frac} of expected bandwidth across nodes. NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shows some ranks using a NIC on the other CPU socket. Explain and fix.
L4.answer: Those ranks' GPUDirect RDMA path crosses the inter-socket interconnect rather than staying under a shared PCIe switch, so their effective bandwidth is a fraction of the NIC rate and, because a collective proceeds at the pace of its slowest participant, they drag the whole all-reduce down. Intra-node traffic is unaffected because it uses NVLink and never touches the NIC. Fix: pin each rank to the NIC under its own PCIe switch, using NCCL_IB_HCA to name the correct device per rank and CPU affinity to keep the process on the matching socket; verify by re-reading the NCCL_DEBUG=INFO topology and confirming every rank reports a local NIC.
L4.explanation: The asymmetry between intra-node and inter-node performance is the diagnostic signature: intra-node uses NVLink and is unaffected by PCIe placement, so a gap between the two points at the NIC-to-GPU path specifically.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why GPUDirect RDMA can be enabled and reported as working while delivering a small fraction of the expected bandwidth, and name the check that settles it.
L4.answer: The feature is a capability, not a path guarantee. If the NIC and GPU are under the same PCIe switch, peer-to-peer DMA never involves the CPU and runs at PCIe link rate. If they are on different root complexes, the same API succeeds and the same code path is taken, but the transfer traverses the inter-socket interconnect, whose peer-to-peer throughput is far below its memory bandwidth and on some platforms is severely limited. Nothing reports an error; the transfer is simply slow. The check is to read the actual topology: nvidia-smi topo -m shows the connection class between each GPU and each NIC, and NCCL_DEBUG=INFO prints the path NCCL selected per rank.
L4.explanation: This is the general shape of GPU-cluster debugging: the API tells you a feature is available, the topology tells you what it will cost. Always read the topology output rather than the capability flag.

sections.note: A collective is a communication pattern with a cost model. Learn the cost model and the training-job questions answer themselves.

concepts.t: The collective primitives and their volumes

L0.body:
n ranks, each holding S bytes. What each primitive produces, and the bytes
one rank must move (ring/bandwidth-optimal implementation):

  broadcast       one rank's S      -> everyone        (n-1)/n * S
  reduce          sum of all S      -> one rank        (n-1)/n * S
  all-gather      each rank's S/n   -> everyone gets S (n-1)/n * S
  reduce-scatter  sum of all S      -> rank i gets S/n (n-1)/n * S
  all-reduce      sum of all S      -> everyone gets S 2(n-1)/n * S
  all-to-all      rank i's j-th S/n -> rank j          (n-1)/n * S

  all_reduce == reduce_scatter ; all_gather      <- the key identity
  torch.distributed.all_reduce(t, op=ReduceOp.SUM)   # in-place, on all ranks
L0.cloze:
An all-reduce is exactly a {{c1::reduce-scatter}} followed by an all-gather, which is why it costs {{c2::twice}} what either costs alone.
All-gather and reduce-scatter each move $\frac{n-1}{n}S$ bytes per rank; all-reduce moves {{c3::$2\frac{n-1}{n}S$}}.
The output of an all-gather has size {{c4::$S$}} on every rank, while the output of a reduce-scatter has size {{c5::$S/n$}}.

concepts.L1: The six collectives every training job uses, with the byte cost each imposes on one rank. All of them are defined by what ends up where, not by how the bytes get there, so the same collective has several implementations with different cost curves.
concepts.L2: People read the cost as proportional to the number of ranks. It is not: every factor above converges to a constant as $n$ grows, $\frac{n-1}{n} \to 1$ and $2\frac{n-1}{n} \to 2$. Doubling the cluster does not double all-reduce bytes.
concepts.L3: Take reduce-scatter: split each rank's $S$ into $n$ chunks. Rank $i$ must end up holding the sum of chunk $i$ across all ranks. Chunk $i$ exists on $n$ ranks and must reach one, so $n-1$ copies of an $S/n$ chunk must cross the fabric per chunk; with $n$ chunks in flight, one rank sends $n-1$ chunks of $S/n$, i.e. $\frac{n-1}{n}S$. All-gather is the same argument reversed. All-reduce is their composition, hence $2\frac{n-1}{n}S$. At $n = 8$ that factor is $1.75$; at $n = 1024$ it is $1.998$. Both are within a factor of two of the $n=2$ case.

L4.prompt_tpl: For an all-reduce of {S} GB across {n} ranks, compute the bytes one rank moves in a bandwidth-optimal implementation, to three decimal places.
L4.explanation: The factor $2\frac{n-1}{n}$ rises from 1.75 at 8 ranks to 1.996 at 512 and never reaches 2. All-reduce cost is essentially independent of cluster size, which is the whole reason data parallelism scales at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using the identity that an all-reduce is a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, derive the ratio of all-reduce cost to {other} cost for any n, and state whether it depends on n. Answer with the ratio.
L4.answer: The ratio is exactly 2, independent of n. All-gather and reduce-scatter each move (n-1)/n * S per rank; all-reduce is their composition and moves 2(n-1)/n * S. The (n-1)/n factor cancels.
L4.explanation: This is why ZeRO-3 and FSDP are not free: replacing one all-reduce with a reduce-scatter of gradients plus an all-gather of parameters moves the same total bytes, and buys memory rather than time.

L4.prompt_tpl: A step currently does an all-reduce of the full gradient on every rank. The team proposes replacing it with {alt}. State the effect on bytes moved and on memory.

alt: reduce-scatter only, sharding the optimiser state

L4.answer: Reduce-scatter plus all-gather moves exactly the same bytes as the all-reduce it replaces, because that decomposition is what a ring all-reduce already does internally; it changes nothing unless you exploit the gap between the two halves. Reduce-scatter only, with sharded optimiser state, halves the collective bytes to (n-1)/n * S and cuts optimiser memory by a factor of n, at the price of needing an all-gather of parameters later in the step. The bytes reappear there, but they are parameter bytes rather than gradient bytes and can overlap with compute.
L4.explanation: The identity all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather is the foundation of ZeRO. Sharding is not a bandwidth saving on its own; it is a memory saving that lets you place the two halves at different points in the step.

L0.body:
n ranks in a logical ring. Each rank's buffer is split into n chunks.

  phase 1  reduce-scatter, n-1 steps
     step k: rank i sends chunk (i-k) mod n to rank i+1, adds what it receives
     after n-1 steps rank i owns the fully reduced chunk i

  phase 2  all-gather, n-1 steps
     step k: rank i forwards the finished chunk it holds to rank i+1
     after n-1 steps every rank holds every finished chunk

  steps  = 2(n-1)            bytes per step per rank = S/n
  time   = 2(n-1)*alpha + 2 * (n-1)/n * S/B

  n=8, S=1 GiB, B=25 GB/s -> 14 steps, 75.16 ms, busbw 25.00 GB/s
L0.cloze:
A ring all-reduce runs in {{c1::$2(n-1)$}} steps, each moving {{c2::$S/n$}} bytes across each link.
Its bandwidth term is {{c3::$2\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac{S}{B}$}} and its latency term is $2(n-1)\alpha$.
Because each rank sends and receives simultaneously on distinct links, the ring uses only {{c4::neighbour}} links and never loads the fabric bisection.
nccl-tests reports algbw $= S/t$ and busbw $=$ algbw $\times$ {{c5::$2\frac{n-1}{n}$}}, so busbw is comparable across $n$.

concepts.L1: The bandwidth-optimal all-reduce: arrange ranks in a ring, split the buffer into $n$ chunks, and pipeline a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather. Every link carries traffic in every step, and no rank is ever idle.
concepts.L2: The ring is bandwidth-optimal but latency-terrible: its step count grows as $2(n-1)$, linearly in the cluster, so at $n=512$ it pays 1022 serialised latencies where a tree pays 18. The bandwidth term barely moves; the latency term is what kills small messages.
concepts.L3: Why $2\frac{n-1}{n}$ and not $2$: in the reduce-scatter phase each of the $n-1$ steps moves one chunk of $S/n$ bytes out of each rank, so a rank sends $(n-1) \cdot S/n$ bytes, not $S$. The all-gather phase repeats it. Total per rank is $2\frac{n-1}{n}S$. Divide by per-link bandwidth $B$ for the time. The busbw metric in nccl-tests exists precisely to undo this factor: it multiplies the observed $S/t$ by $2\frac{n-1}{n}$ so that a healthy fabric reports a number close to the link rate at every $n$, and a sagging curve means a real problem rather than a larger ring.

L4.prompt_tpl: Ring all-reduce of {S} MB over {n} ranks with {B} GB/s per link and negligible latency. Give the time in milliseconds.
L4.explanation: Note the units cancel: MB divided by GB/s is milliseconds. Doubling ranks from 8 to 64 costs 12.5 percent more time; doubling bandwidth halves it. Bandwidth is the lever, rank count is not.

L4.prompt_tpl: nccl-tests reports algbw {a} GB/s for an all-reduce over {n} ranks. Compute the busbw it will print, and say which of the two you should compare against the link rate. Answer with the busbw in GB/s.
L4.answer: busbw = algbw * 2(n-1)/n. a=14.2857,n=8: 25.000 GB/s. a=14.2857,n=64: 28.125 GB/s. a=12.6984,n=8: 22.222. a=12.6984,n=64: 25.000. a=7.0,n=8: 12.250. a=7.0,n=64: 13.781. Compare busbw against the link rate: algbw is deflated by the algorithm factor and would make every large ring look broken.
L4.explanation: algbw is what the application sees; busbw is what the wire sees. A busbw plateau near the link rate at large message sizes means the fabric is healthy, so a busbw curve that sags at large sizes points at the fabric rather than at the collective.

L4.prompt_tpl: A ring all-reduce over {n} ranks reaches only a fraction of link rate, and NCCL reports one rank on a slower path. Explain the effect on total time and why the ring amplifies it.
L4.answer: Every step of the ring is a synchronised exchange: a rank cannot forward chunk k+1 until it has received and reduced chunk k. One slow link therefore sets the pace of every one of the 2(n-1) steps, so the whole collective runs at the slow link's rate rather than losing only its share. With n=8 that is 14 steps at the wrong rate, with n=64 it is 126, with n=512 it is 1022. The ring has no alternative path, so there is no way for the fast links to absorb the difference; unlike ECMP, where a collision costs one flow, a ring collision costs the collective.
L4.explanation: This is why NCCL topology output matters more than aggregate fabric bandwidth. A collective is a synchronised pipeline, so its throughput is the minimum link rate, not the mean.

concepts.t: Tree, recursive halving-doubling, and the crossover

L0.body:
Three all-reduce algorithms, same result, different cost shape:

  ring    steps 2(n-1)        bytes 2(n-1)/n * S     bandwidth-optimal
  RHD     steps 2*log2(n)     bytes 2(n-1)/n * S     both, for power-of-two n
  tree    steps 2*log2(n)     bytes 2S per rank      latency-optimal

  RHD = recursive-halving reduce-scatter + recursive-doubling all-gather
        (Rabenseifner). Step k exchanges with the rank differing in bit k.

  n=64, alpha=5 us, B=25 GB/s:
     S=1 KB    ring 630.08 us   RHD  60.08 us    ring is 10.5x worse
     S=1 MB    ring 712.58 us   RHD 142.58 us    ring is 5.0x worse
     S=64 MB   ring 5914.8 us   RHD 5344.8 us    ring is 1.11x worse
L0.cloze:
The ring costs {{c1::$2(n-1)$}} serialised steps; recursive halving-doubling and the tree cost {{c2::$2\log_{2} n$}}.
Rabenseifner's algorithm is both latency- and bandwidth-optimal for {{c3::power-of-two}} rank counts.
A plain binomial tree is latency-optimal but not bandwidth-optimal: the root moves {{c4::$2S$}} bytes rather than $2\frac{n-1}{n}S$.
NCCL therefore chooses tree for {{c5::small}} messages and ring for large ones.

concepts.L1: The same all-reduce has a latency-dominated regime and a bandwidth-dominated regime, and different algorithms win in each. Cost is $\text{steps} \cdot \alpha + \text{bytes}/B$; algorithms trade one term against the other.
concepts.L2: The tree is not simply better despite having fewer steps. A binomial tree concentrates traffic on the root and its immediate children, so its bandwidth term does not carry the $\frac{n-1}{n}$ discount and it saturates a single link at large $S$. Fewer steps is not fewer bytes.
concepts.L3: Set the two costs equal. Ring: $2(n-1)\alpha + 2\frac{n-1}{n}\frac{S}{B}$. RHD: $2\log_{2}(n)\alpha + 2\frac{n-1}{n}\frac{S}{B}$. The bandwidth terms are identical, so RHD is never worse in this model and the whole difference is $2(n-1-\log_{2} n)\alpha$, a constant. Against a plain tree the trade is real: the tree saves latency but pays $2S/B$ instead of $2\frac{n-1}{n}S/B$, so the crossover sits where $2(n-1-\log_{2}n)\alpha = 2S/B \cdot (1 - \frac{n-1}{n})$. With $n=64$, $\alpha=5\,\mu$s and $B=25$ GB/s that lands in the low megabytes, which is exactly where NCCL's measured tree-to-ring switch sits.

L4.prompt_tpl: With alpha = {alpha} microseconds and n = {n} ranks, compute the pure latency cost in microseconds of a ring all-reduce and of a log-depth all-reduce, and give the ratio. Answer with the ratio of ring latency to log-depth latency.
L4.answer: ring = 2(n-1)*alpha, log = 2*log2(n)*alpha, ratio = (n-1)/log2(n). alpha=5,n=64: ring 630 us, log 60 us, ratio 10.50. alpha=5,n=512: ring 5110 us, log 90 us, ratio 56.78. alpha=2,n=64: ring 252 us, log 24 us, ratio 10.50. alpha=2,n=512: ring 2044 us, log 36 us, ratio 56.78. The ratio is independent of alpha.
L4.explanation: The ratio $(n-1)/\log_{2} n$ is why the ring is unusable for small tensors at scale: at 512 ranks it pays 57 times the latency for no bandwidth benefit at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rank count is {n}. Pick ring or tree for an all-reduce of {S}, and justify from the cost model rather than from a benchmark.
L4.answer: For the 4 KB bucket, choose the tree: the bandwidth term is negligible at any n, so cost is dominated by step count, and the tree pays 2*log2(n) steps against the ring's 2(n-1) -- 12 versus 126 at n=64, 18 versus 1022 at n=512. For the 512 MB bucket, choose the ring: the latency difference is a fixed few hundred microseconds to a few milliseconds, while the tree's bandwidth term is 2S/B rather than 2(n-1)/n * S/B and concentrates that traffic on the root's links, so at half a gigabyte the ring wins by a wide margin at both rank counts.
L4.explanation: The decision rule is the ratio of the two terms, not the absolute size. Ask which term dominates at this message size and this rank count, then pick the algorithm that optimises that term.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team sets NCCL_ALGO={algo} globally to make their training deterministic, and reports that {sym}. Identify the mistake.

sym: large all-reduces lost half their bandwidth

L4.answer: Pinning NCCL_ALGO removes the per-message-size selection that is the point of NCCL's tuner. Forcing Ring makes every small collective pay 2(n-1) serialised steps instead of 2*log2(n), which is the small-tensor slowdown. Forcing Tree makes every large all-reduce pay 2S/B on the root's links instead of the ring's 2(n-1)/n * S/B spread over all links, which is the lost bandwidth. Determinism in reduction order is a separate concern and is not what NCCL_ALGO controls; if bitwise reproducibility is the goal, fix the reduction order and precision explicitly rather than the algorithm.
L4.explanation: NCCL_ALGO is a debugging instrument: set it to confirm a hypothesis about which regime you are in, then unset it. A permanently pinned algorithm is a permanent tax at one end of the message-size range.

concepts.t: All-to-all, and the cost of expert parallelism

L0.body:
all-to-all: rank i sends a distinct S/n slice to every rank j.

  egress per rank  = (n-1)/n * S        (same as all-gather)
  fabric total     = (n-1) * S
  BISECTION load   = (n/2)*(n/2)*(S/n) = n*S/4    <- grows LINEARLY in n

  compare ring all-reduce: neighbour links only, bisection load ~ 0

  MoE step: dispatch tokens to experts, then combine results back.
  Two all-to-alls per MoE layer.
    T=8192 tokens, h=4096, bf16, n=64 experts-parallel ranks:
      one all-to-all = 8192*4096*2*63/64 = 66.060 MB egress per rank
      dispatch + combine                 = 132.121 MB per rank per layer
L0.cloze:
An all-to-all moves {{c1::$\frac{n-1}{n}S$}} bytes out of each rank, the same as an all-gather, but it loads the fabric bisection with {{c2::$nS/4$}} bytes, which grows linearly in $n$.
A ring all-reduce loads the bisection with essentially {{c3::nothing}}, because it only uses neighbour links.
An MoE layer costs {{c4::two}} all-to-alls per forward pass: dispatch and combine.
This is why expert parallelism is usually confined to {{c5::one node}} or one rail, where bandwidth is cheap.

concepts.L1: The collective in which every rank sends different data to every other rank. Per-rank egress matches all-gather, but unlike all-gather it cannot be arranged as neighbour traffic, so it is the only common collective whose cost is set by fabric bisection rather than by link rate.
concepts.L2: The trap is comparing all-to-all with all-reduce by egress bytes and concluding it is cheaper. Egress is smaller, but a ring all-reduce is neighbour-local while all-to-all is uniform random, so on an oversubscribed fabric the all-to-all is the one that collapses.
concepts.L3: Count what crosses the bisection. Cut the $n$ ranks into halves of $n/2$. In an all-to-all each of the $n/2$ ranks on the left sends $S/n$ to each of the $n/2$ ranks on the right: $(n/2)(n/2)(S/n) = nS/4$ bytes across the cut, in each direction. At $n=64$ that is $16S$; at $n=1024$ it is $256S$. A ring embedded so that neighbours are physically adjacent crosses the cut exactly twice regardless of $n$. So all-to-all is the collective that turns an oversubscription ratio into a training-throughput number, and it is why a 4:1 oversubscribed spine that is invisible to data-parallel jobs becomes the binding constraint the moment experts are sharded across pods.

L4.prompt_tpl: An MoE layer with T = {T} tokens per rank, hidden {h}, bf16, sharded over {n} expert-parallel ranks. Compute the egress bytes per rank per layer, in MB, counting both dispatch and combine.
L4.explanation: The factor 2 outside is dispatch plus combine; the factor 2 inside is bf16. Note this is per MoE layer, so a model with dozens of MoE layers multiplies it, and unlike an all-reduce none of it overlaps with the backward pass.

L4.prompt_tpl: For {n} ranks each holding S bytes, derive the bytes crossing a bisection cut for an all-to-all and for a ring all-reduce, and give the ratio. Answer with the all-to-all bisection bytes as a multiple of S.
L4.answer: All-to-all: (n/2)*(n/2)*(S/n) = nS/4. n=8: 2S. n=64: 16S. n=1024: 256S. Ring all-reduce with neighbours physically adjacent: the ring crosses the cut twice, so 2 * (S/n) per step over 2(n-1) steps, i.e. about 4S total, independent of n. Ratio at n=8 is about 0.5, at n=64 about 4, at n=1024 about 64. The all-to-all grows linearly in n; the ring does not grow at all.
L4.explanation: This single comparison explains why data parallelism tolerates an oversubscribed spine and expert parallelism does not. The ring was designed to keep traffic local; all-to-all has no locality to exploit.

L4.prompt_tpl: A cluster has full bandwidth within a node and {ratio} oversubscription between pods. Decide where to place the expert-parallel dimension of an MoE model and justify with the bisection argument.
L4.answer: Place expert parallelism entirely inside a node, or at most inside a single non-oversubscribed pod. All-to-all loads the bisection with nS/4 bytes, so it runs at the oversubscribed rate rather than the link rate the moment it spans pods: at 4:1 the collective takes four times as long, at 8:1 eight times, and at 2:1 twice. Data parallelism should take the oversubscribed dimension instead, because a ring all-reduce is neighbour-local and its bisection load does not grow with rank count. The general rule: assign the all-to-all dimension to the fattest, least oversubscribed level of the hierarchy, and the all-reduce dimension to the thinnest.
L4.explanation: Parallelism placement is a mapping from collectives to levels of the network hierarchy. Get it backwards and the fabric's cheapest dimension carries the traffic that needs bisection.

concepts.t: Parallelism strategy is a choice of collective

L0.body:
Each parallelism axis is defined by the collective it forces, and by how often:

  data parallel (DDP)   all-reduce of gradients      once per step, size = params
  ZeRO-2 / FSDP         reduce-scatter grads +
                        all-gather params            per bucket, per step
  tensor parallel (TP)  all-reduce of activations    TWICE per transformer layer
  pipeline parallel     point-to-point send/recv     per micro-batch boundary
  sequence / context    all-gather + reduce-scatter  per attention block
  expert parallel (MoE) all-to-all dispatch+combine  twice per MoE layer

  TP all-reduce, 4096 tokens, h=8192, bf16 -> S = 67.109 MB per layer
     over NVLink at 450 GB/s : 260.98 us
     over 200 GbE at  25 GB/s: 4697.62 us       -> 18x, hence TP stays in-node
L0.cloze:
Data parallelism forces one {{c1::all-reduce}} per step, sized by the parameter count.
Tensor parallelism forces an all-reduce {{c2::twice}} per transformer layer, sized by the activations, which is why it is confined to a single {{c3::node}} on NVLink.
Pipeline parallelism uses only {{c4::point-to-point}} sends, which is why it tolerates the slowest links in the cluster.
Expert parallelism forces {{c5::all-to-all}}, the one collective whose cost is set by fabric bisection.

concepts.L1: The parallelism strategy you choose is, mechanically, a choice about which collective runs how often on which part of the network. Every placement decision in a training job reduces to matching a collective's cost shape to a level of the fabric hierarchy.
concepts.L2: The usual framing treats parallelism as a memory-fitting exercise and network cost as an afterthought. It is the reverse: the memory question usually has several answers, and the network cost is what eliminates all but one of them.
concepts.L3: Compare frequencies, not sizes. Data-parallel all-reduce runs once per step: 140 GB for a 70B bf16 model, but once, overlapping the backward pass. Tensor-parallel all-reduce runs twice per layer over activations; at 4096 tokens and $h = 8192$ that is 67 MB, tiny by comparison, but with 80 layers it fires 160 times per pass and cannot overlap, since the next op consumes its result. At 450 GB/s NVLink each costs 261 microseconds, 42 ms per pass; over a 25 GB/s link each costs 4.70 ms, 752 ms, which would dominate the step. That ratio is why TP degree never exceeds the NVLink domain, and why pipeline parallelism, needing only point-to-point sends, is the axis you stretch across your slowest links.

L4.prompt_tpl: Tensor-parallel all-reduce of activations: {tok} tokens, hidden {h}, bf16, {n}-way TP. Compute the bytes moved per rank per all-reduce, in MB.
L4.explanation: Per-all-reduce this looks small, but it fires twice per layer and cannot be overlapped, because the next matmul consumes the reduced activation. Multiply by twice the layer count before comparing with the data-parallel all-reduce.

L4.prompt_tpl: A model has {L} transformer layers. Compare total TP all-reduce time per forward pass at 450 GB/s NVLink and at 25 GB/s Ethernet, for 4096 tokens, h = 8192, 8-way TP. Give both totals in milliseconds. Answer with the NVLink total in milliseconds.
L4.answer: Per all-reduce: 2*(n-1)/n*S/B with S = 67.109 MB. NVLink: 0.26098 ms. Ethernet: 4.69762 ms. Two per layer. L=80: 41.76 ms vs 751.62 ms. L=32: 16.70 ms vs 300.65 ms. L=126: 65.77 ms vs 1183.80 ms.
L4.explanation: The ratio is fixed at 18, the bandwidth ratio, but the absolute numbers are what decide the design: a second of network time per forward pass is not a tax you can pay, so TP degree is bounded by the NVLink domain size.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must train a model that does not fit in one node, on a cluster of 8-GPU NVLink nodes joined by {fabric}. Assign the parallelism axes to the levels of the hierarchy and justify each from its collective.
L4.answer: Tensor parallelism goes inside the node, degree at most 8: its all-reduce fires twice per layer on activations and cannot overlap with compute, so it needs NVLink bandwidth and would cost roughly 18 times more on any inter-node link. Pipeline parallelism takes the worst links available, because it uses only point-to-point sends at micro-batch boundaries and its cost is a small number of large transfers that pipeline with compute. Data parallelism takes the remaining inter-node dimension: its all-reduce is neighbour-local in a ring, does not load the bisection, and overlaps with the backward pass. On the oversubscribed spine, keep the data-parallel ring inside pods where possible and never place an all-to-all across pods; on the non-blocking fabric the data-parallel and pipeline dimensions can span the whole cluster freely.
L4.explanation: The mapping is always the same: highest-frequency, non-overlappable collective goes on the fattest link; point-to-point goes on the thinnest; bisection-hungry all-to-all goes wherever there is no oversubscription.

L0.body:
NCCL builds rings and trees from a topology it DISCOVERS at init, then tunes.

  NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,GRAPH,NET,TUNING ./train.py
  ... NCCL INFO Channel 00/12 : 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7      <- the ring it chose
  ... NCCL INFO NET/IB : Using [0]mlx5_0:1/RoCE       <- the NIC per rank
  ... NCCL INFO Setting affinity for GPU 0 to 0-23

  protocols, by bytes on the wire per byte of payload:
    LL      4-byte data + 4-byte flag   -> 50.0 %  efficient, lowest latency
    LL128   120 data per 128-byte line  -> 93.75 % efficient, needs NVLink
    Simple  full payload, memory fences -> 100 %   efficient, highest latency

  NCCL_BUFFSIZE  per-connection, per-channel staging buffer (4 MiB default)
  NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS / NCCL_MAX_NCHANNELS  parallel rings over the same ranks
L0.cloze:
NCCL discovers topology at {{c1::init}} time and prints its chosen rings under NCCL_DEBUG=INFO.
The LL protocol pairs each 4 bytes of data with a 4-byte flag, so its wire efficiency is {{c2::50}} percent.
LL128 packs 120 payload bytes into a 128-byte line, for {{c3::93.75}} percent.
Channels are {{c4::parallel}} rings over the same ranks, used to fill a link that one ring cannot saturate.
NCCL_BUFFSIZE is charged {{c5::per channel}}, so raising channels and buffer size together multiplies memory.

concepts.L1: NCCL is a topology-discovery engine with collectives attached. At initialisation it reads PCIe, NVLink and NIC topology, constructs rings and trees over it, picks a protocol and channel count per message size, and only then moves bytes.
concepts.L2: Engineers treat NCCL_BUFFSIZE and NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS as independent throughput knobs. They multiply: memory is roughly buffsize $\times$ channels $\times$ peers, so raising both on a large ring can consume gigabytes of GPU memory and cause an out-of-memory error far from the change.
concepts.L3: Why three protocols rather than one. LL (low latency) writes 8-byte units where 4 bytes are payload and 4 are a flag the receiver polls; no memory fence is needed because the flag's arrival proves the data arrived, so latency is minimal but half the wire is wasted. LL128 exploits the fact that NVLink transfers 128-byte lines atomically: 120 payload bytes plus an 8-byte flag gives 93.75 percent efficiency with the same fence-free property, but it is only correct where that atomicity holds. Simple uses the whole payload and pays a memory fence per step: full efficiency, highest latency. NCCL picks by message size and link type, so forcing NCCL_PROTO globally costs you at one end of the range.

L4.prompt_tpl: A collective moves {S} MB of payload using the {proto} protocol. Compute the bytes actually placed on the wire, in MB.
L4.explanation: LL doubles the bytes on the wire to remove a memory fence, which is a good trade only while the message is small enough that latency dominates. Above that point the doubled bandwidth cost is the whole story.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team raises NCCL_BUFFSIZE to {buf} and NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS to {ch} on a {n}-rank job to 'get more bandwidth', and the job now fails with a CUDA out-of-memory error during the first collective. Explain.
L4.answer: The staging buffer is allocated per channel per connection, not once. Raising both multiplies: buffer size times channel count times the number of peers a rank talks to. At 16 MiB and 16 channels a rank with 8 peers is already reserving on the order of 2 GB of GPU memory before a single byte of payload moves, and at 32 MiB with 32 channels it is several times that. The allocation happens lazily at the first collective, which is why the failure appears far from the configuration change. Raise one knob at a time, measure with nccl-tests, and check the reported memory in NCCL_DEBUG=INFO output.
L4.explanation: The general failure mode: NCCL tuning knobs are per-connection, and connection count grows with rank count. Any knob you set is multiplied by a number that changes when the job is resized.

L4.prompt_tpl: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO shows {obs}. State what it tells you and the next thing to check.

obs: different ranks using different mlx5 devices

L4.answer: NET/Socket means NCCL fell back to TCP sockets instead of RDMA: the verbs library or device was not visible to the process, so check that the container exposes /dev/infiniband, that libibverbs is present, and that NCCL_IB_DISABLE is not set. Different mlx5 devices per rank is normal and correct on a multi-rail node, and is what you want; the thing to check is that each rank's device is the one under its own PCIe switch, using nvidia-smi topo -m. Two channels where more were expected means NCCL found little parallelism in the discovered topology, usually because it saw one NIC or one PCIe path; check the topology dump before raising NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS, because forcing channels onto a path that does not exist does not create bandwidth.
L4.explanation: Read the init output as a claim about the machine, then verify that claim against the hardware. Almost every NCCL performance problem is a discrepancy between what NCCL discovered and what the node actually is.

L0.body:
A collective is a barrier. Any rank that does not arrive hangs ALL of them.

  the four causes, in order of how often they actually happen:

  1 divergent control flow   one rank took an if-branch that skipped the
                             collective, or called them in a different ORDER
  2 mismatched shapes/dtype  all_reduce of 1024 floats on rank 0 and 512 on
                             rank 3 -> NCCL blocks, no error
  3 a dead peer              a rank OOMed or segfaulted; the rest wait forever
  4 fabric loss with no CC   an RDMA send never completes; PFC pause storm

  first three commands, always the same:
    py-spy dump --pid <each rank>          where is every rank stuck?
    NCCL_DEBUG=INFO + TORCH_NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1
    check dmesg and the NIC counters for PFC pause frames
L0.cloze:
A collective is a {{c1::barrier}}: every rank must call it, with matching shape and dtype, in the same {{c2::order}}.
The most common hang is not a network fault but {{c3::divergent control flow}} on one rank.
A shape mismatch does not raise an error; NCCL simply {{c4::blocks}}.
The diagnostic that separates a network hang from a program hang is to dump the {{c5::stack}} of every rank and see whether they are all inside NCCL.

concepts.L1: Collectives fail by hanging rather than by erroring, because a collective has no way to know the difference between a peer that is slow and a peer that will never arrive. Diagnosis is therefore a process of finding the rank that is somewhere else.
concepts.L2: The instinct is to blame the fabric, since the symptom is a stalled network call. In practice the fabric is the least common cause: a rank that took a different branch, or called collectives in a different order, produces exactly the same stall with no packet loss anywhere.
concepts.L3: Why order matters and not just presence. NCCL matches operations positionally on a communicator, not by name or tag. If rank 0 issues all-reduce then all-gather while rank 1 issues all-gather then all-reduce, rank 0's all-reduce is matched against rank 1's all-gather; the shapes disagree, and both block. The same mechanism turns a data-dependent branch into a hang: a rank that skips a collective shifts every later operation by one, so the job runs a while and then stalls at an unrelated line. Hence the stack dump first: all ranks at the same call means suspect the fabric; a rank elsewhere, or ranks at different calls, means the bug is in the program and no NCCL tuning will find it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A job hangs after {steps} steps. A stack dump shows {obs}. Give the diagnosis and the fix.

obs: all ranks inside ncclAllReduce at the same source line
rank 5 inside a dataloader worker, all others inside ncclAllReduce
ranks 0-3 in ncclAllReduce and ranks 4-7 in ncclAllGather

L4.answer: All ranks at the same NCCL call means the program is consistent and the fault is below it: check NIC counters for PFC pause frames and RDMA completion errors, check that every rank resolved an RDMA path rather than falling back to sockets, and look for a link that went down. One rank elsewhere means that rank never arrived: it is stuck or dead upstream of the collective, so read its stack, and if it is in a dataloader suspect a blocking read or an exhausted worker rather than the network. Ranks at different collectives is divergent control flow: some ranks executed a conditional the others did not, so the operations are matched pairwise against the wrong partners. The fix for the last case is to make the collective unconditional, or to all-reduce the branch condition first so every rank agrees before diverging.
L4.explanation: The stack dump partitions the space in one step: same call is a fabric question, one rank missing is a process question, different calls is a program-logic question. Nothing else discriminates as cheaply.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team sets a {timeout} NCCL/process-group timeout to stop hangs from wasting cluster hours. Evaluate the choice and its failure modes.
L4.answer: A timeout converts a silent hang into a crash with a stack, which is a real improvement, but the value has to sit above the slowest legitimate collective. Thirty seconds is too short: checkpoint writes, the first collective after initialisation, and elastic rendezvous can all exceed it, so the job dies on healthy behaviour and the team learns to raise it blindly. Twenty-four hours is too long to be useful; the hang has already cost what you were trying to save. Ten minutes is a defensible default for large jobs. In all cases enable async error handling so the timeout aborts the process group and prints the offending collective, and log the rank and operation, because the timeout's value is the diagnostic it produces, not the hours it saves.
L4.explanation: The timeout is an observability mechanism first and a cost control second. Set it so that it fires only on real hangs, and make sure it prints which collective and which rank, or you have swapped a hang for an unexplained crash.

concepts.t: tcpdump: what is actually on the wire

L0.body:
tcpdump -i any -nn -s0 -w cap.pcap 'tcp port 5432 and host 10.0.3.7'

    -i any   all interfaces      -nn  never resolve names OR ports
    -s0      full packet         -w   raw pcap, read it later

  Read it back, one line per packet, with relative sequence numbers:

  tcpdump -r cap.pcap -nn -tttt
  10:14:02.001 IP 10.0.3.7.51234 > 10.0.1.4.5432: Flags [S],  seq 1, win 64240
  10:14:02.041 IP 10.0.1.4.5432 > 10.0.3.7.51234: Flags [S.], seq 1, ack 1
  10:14:02.041 IP 10.0.3.7.51234 > 10.0.1.4.5432: Flags [.],  ack 1
  10:14:02.083 IP 10.0.3.7.51234 > 10.0.1.4.5432: Flags [P.], seq 1:88

  Flags: S=SYN  S.=SYN-ACK  P=PSH  F=FIN  R=RST  .=ACK only

  Retransmit = the same seq sent twice. tcpdump will not tell you; you look.
L0.cloze:
Always pass {{c1::-nn}} so tcpdump does not do DNS lookups that generate the traffic you are trying to capture.
The flag notation shows a SYN-ACK as {{c2::[S.]}}, where the dot means an ACK is also set.
A capture written with {{c3::-w}} is raw pcap and keeps everything; the printed form is lossy.
The filter is a {{c4::BPF}} expression compiled into the kernel, so packets that do not match are never copied to userspace.
A retransmission appears as the same {{c5::sequence number}} sent twice, which you must spot yourself.

concepts.L1: The instrument that answers 'what left this machine and what arrived'. It attaches a kernel BPF filter to a capture socket, so filtering happens before the copy to userspace and a narrow filter costs almost nothing on a busy host.
concepts.L2: A capture without a filter on a loaded host drops packets, and tcpdump reports those drops in one line at exit that everyone ignores. A capture that silently dropped 40 percent of packets looks exactly like a network that dropped them.
concepts.L3: Two habits separate useful captures from useless ones. First, filter in the kernel, not in your eyes: the BPF expression is compiled and run per packet in the kernel, costing a few instructions, while capturing everything and grepping later forces a copy of every packet through a userspace ring buffer that will overflow. Second, capture on both ends. tcpdump on the sender proves a packet was transmitted; only a capture on the receiver proves it arrived. A packet present at the sender and absent at the receiver localises the loss to the path between them, a fact no single-ended capture can establish and the one that ends most arguments between teams.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must find why {sym} on a host carrying 400k packets per second. Write the tcpdump invocation you would run and justify each flag.

sym: a service sees resets it did not send

L4.answer:
Something of the form: tcpdump -i any -nn -s0 -c 20000 -w cap.pcap 'host and tcp port

'. The narrow host-and-port filter is the important part, because at 400k pps an unfiltered capture will overflow the ring buffer and drop packets that you will then misread as network loss. -nn prevents DNS lookups, which both slow the capture and inject traffic. -s0 keeps full payload, needed to see TLS record types or an application-level cause of a reset. -w writes raw pcap so you can re-filter later without recapturing. -c bounds the file. For the reset case, capture on both endpoints, because a reset seen at the client but never sent by the server means a middlebox generated it.
L4.explanation: The decision is always the same: narrow the BPF filter until the capture is cheap, keep full packets, write raw, and capture on both ends whenever the question is whether something arrived.

L4.prompt_tpl: A capture shows {obs}. State what happened and what to check next.

obs: Flags [S] sent three times at 1s, 3s, 7s with no reply
Flags [R] from the server immediately after [S.] and [.]
the same seq 4400:5860 sent twice, 210 ms apart

L4.answer: Three SYNs at exponentially growing intervals with no reply is the SYN retransmission timer: nothing is answering, so either a firewall is dropping silently rather than rejecting, or the destination has no listener and the RST is being filtered, or the route is wrong. Check reachability at L3 and whether the listener exists on the server. A reset immediately after a completed handshake is the application refusing: the connection was accepted by the kernel and then closed, so look at the server process, its accept backlog, and any TLS or protocol check that runs before the first byte. The same sequence range sent twice 210 ms apart is a retransmission after an RTO, not a fast retransmit, since a fast retransmit follows three duplicate ACKs within roughly one RTT; check whether the receiver's ACK was lost or the data was, by capturing at the receiver.
L4.explanation: Retransmission timing classifies the loss: an RTO-spaced retransmit means no feedback arrived at all, while a fast retransmit means later packets got through. The two point at different parts of the path.

  ss -s                         summary counts by state

  ss -ti shows the congestion-control state the kernel is really using:

  ESTAB 0 0  10.0.3.7:51234  10.0.1.4:5432
     cubic rto:244 rtt:41.2/2.1 mss:1448 cwnd:42 ssthresh:31
     bytes_sent:88123 retrans:0/7 delivery_rate:9.1Mbps

  retrans:0/7   0 retransmitting now, 7 in this socket's lifetime
  cwnd:42       window in SEGMENTS, so 42*1448 = 60816 bytes
  rtt:41.2/2.1  smoothed RTT and its mean deviation, ms

  On a LISTEN socket the two queues change meaning:
    Recv-Q = completed connections waiting for accept()
    Send-Q = the backlog ceiling

`ss -ti` prints per-socket state including cwnd in {{c1::segments}}, not bytes, so multiply by mss to get a window in bytes.
The field `retrans:a/b` gives currently-retransmitting segments and the {{c2::lifetime}} total for that socket.
On a LISTEN socket, Recv-Q is the number of completed connections waiting for {{c3::accept}} and Send-Q is the backlog ceiling.
A non-zero Recv-Q on an established socket means the {{c4::application}} has not read, not that the network is slow.

concepts.L1: The socket-level instrument. Where tcpdump shows packets, `ss` shows the kernel's own control variables for a connection: congestion window, smoothed RTT, retransmit counts, and both queue depths, without capturing anything.
concepts.L2: A full Recv-Q is read as network congestion. It is the opposite: bytes have arrived and the application has not called `read`. The network delivered; the process is the bottleneck, and the sender will stall only later, once the advertised window closes.
concepts.L3: The queue fields are the fastest diagnosis in the toolkit because they say which side of the socket is at fault. On an established socket, Recv-Q counts bytes received by the kernel and not yet read by the application, and Send-Q counts bytes written by the application and not yet acknowledged by the peer. So a large Recv-Q means your process is too slow; a large Send-Q means the peer or the path is. On a LISTEN socket the same columns mean something else: Recv-Q is the completed-connection queue `accept` drains, Send-Q the configured backlog, and Recv-Q equal to Send-Q means connections are being dropped right now, counted as `ListenOverflows`.

L4.prompt_tpl: ss -ti reports cwnd:{cwnd} mss:{mss} rtt:{rtt}. Compute the in-flight window in bytes and the implied throughput ceiling in Mb/s. Answer with the throughput ceiling in Mb/s.
L4.explanation: This is the bandwidth-delay product read backwards: the kernel tells you the window it is willing to keep in flight, and dividing by RTT gives the ceiling that window imposes regardless of how much link capacity exists.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service is slow. ss shows {obs}. Give the diagnosis and say whether the network is implicated.

obs: ESTAB sockets with large Recv-Q and Send-Q 0
a LISTEN socket with Recv-Q equal to Send-Q
ESTAB sockets with Send-Q large and retrans rising

L4.answer: Large Recv-Q with empty Send-Q means data arrived and the application has not read it: the network delivered fine and the process is the bottleneck, so look at thread pools, blocking handlers and event-loop stalls. A LISTEN socket whose Recv-Q has reached Send-Q means the accept queue is full and new completed connections are being dropped or refused right now; confirm with the ListenOverflows counter, then either accept faster or raise the backlog, knowing the backlog only buys time. Large Send-Q with rising retrans is the one case where the network is implicated: the application wrote, the peer has not acknowledged, and segments are being resent, so move to per-hop loss measurement.
L4.explanation: Two columns and one counter separate application slowness, accept-queue exhaustion and genuine path loss. Reach for a packet capture only after this has pointed at the third.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why `ss -ti` reporting retrans:{r} on a socket is not by itself evidence of a network problem, and what would make it evidence.
L4.answer: The second number is a lifetime total for that socket, not a rate. Seven retransmissions over a connection that sent tens of thousands of segments is normal: loss-based congestion control deliberately induces loss to find the path capacity, so a healthy long-lived TCP connection will always show some. Even 1400 is meaningless until divided by bytes_sent or by the segment count. What makes it evidence is a ratio and a comparison: compute retransmitted segments over total segments sent, from /proc/net/snmp for the host or from bytes_retrans over bytes_sent for the socket, and compare it against other sockets on the same host and the same socket at a quieter time. A ratio that is an order of magnitude above its peers is a signal; a raw count is not.
L4.explanation: Every counter in this toolkit is a total. Turn it into a rate or a ratio before drawing any conclusion, and always compare against a control.

socket, bind, listen, accept, and the two queues

concepts.t: Retransmit counters, and locating loss on a path

Host-wide counters, no capture needed. Real numbers from this sandbox:

  grep -A1 '^Tcp:' /proc/net/snmp
  Tcp: ... ActiveOpens PassiveOpens ... InSegs OutSegs RetransSegs ...
  Tcp: ...     32           4       ... 4938   13639      14       ...

    retransmit ratio = 14 / 13639 = 0.1026 %

  nstat -az | grep -E 'TcpExtTCPTimeouts|TcpExtListenOverflows'

  Then localise per hop. mtr probes EVERY hop, continuously:

  mtr -rwzbc 500 10.0.9.31
    HOST         Loss%  Snt  Last   Avg  Wrst
    1. 10.0.0.1   0.0%  500   0.3   0.4   1.9
    2. 10.0.4.1  18.0%  500   1.1   1.4  12.0   <- ICMP rate limit?
    3. 10.0.9.31  0.0%  500   1.4   1.6   9.8   <- the real answer

  Loss at hop k that does NOT persist to hop k+1 is ICMP rate
  limiting, not loss. Only loss reaching the destination is real.
L0.cloze:
The host-wide retransmit ratio is RetransSegs over {{c1::OutSegs}} from /proc/net/snmp, and is meaningful only as a ratio.
`mtr` differs from traceroute by probing every hop {{c2::continuously}}, so it produces a loss percentage per hop rather than one sample.
Loss reported at an intermediate hop that does not appear at later hops is {{c3::ICMP rate limiting}} by that router, not packet loss.
Only loss that {{c4::persists}} to the final hop is real.
Mathis: TCP throughput is bounded by $\frac{MSS}{RTT\sqrt{p}}$, so it falls as {{c5::$1/\sqrt{p}$}} in the loss rate.

concepts.L1: Two counters and one tool. The kernel's own retransmit totals say whether this host is losing packets at all; `mtr` says where on the path it happens. Neither requires a capture, and both can run continuously in production.
concepts.L2: Everyone reads the per-hop Loss column of mtr as loss at that hop. Routers deprioritise and rate-limit the ICMP they generate for their own address while forwarding transit traffic perfectly, so a middle hop showing 18 percent loss with a clean destination is a healthy router that is bored of answering.
concepts.L3: Why loss hurts so much more than intuition suggests: the Mathis model bounds a loss-based TCP flow at $\frac{MSS}{RTT\sqrt{p}}$, where $p$ is the loss probability. Because the dependence is $1/\sqrt{p}$ rather than $1/p$, the damage is front-loaded. With $MSS = 1460$ and $RTT = 80$ ms, a loss rate of $10^{-4}$ permits 14.6 Mb/s, while $10^{-2}$ permits 1.46 Mb/s: a hundredfold rise in loss costs a tenfold fall in throughput, and a link that is 99 percent clean delivers about a tenth of what a 99.99 percent link does. So a fraction of a percent of loss on a long path is a serious fault, not a rounding error.

L4.prompt_tpl: A host reports OutSegs {o} and RetransSegs {r} in /proc/net/snmp. Compute the retransmit ratio as a percentage to four decimal places.
L4.explanation: These are cumulative since boot, so the ratio is a lifetime average and hides bursts. Sample the two counters at an interval and divide the deltas to get the ratio for that window, which is what a real dashboard does.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using the Mathis bound, compute the throughput ceiling in Mb/s for MSS 1460, RTT {rtt} ms, loss probability {p}.
L4.explanation: The bound involves neither link capacity nor the receive window, which is the point: on a lossy long path, buying bandwidth changes nothing and the only levers are loss rate, RTT and a congestion control that is not loss-based.

L4.prompt_tpl: An mtr report to a service shows {obs}. State whether loss is real and what you would do next.

obs: 18 percent at hop 2 and 0 percent at the destination
0.4 percent at hop 4 and 0.4 percent at every hop after it
100 percent at hop 3 with the destination answering normally

L4.answer: Loss at an intermediate hop that vanishes at the destination is not loss: that router rate-limits the ICMP it generates for its own address while forwarding transit traffic normally. Ignore it. Loss that first appears at hop 4 and persists at every subsequent hop, including the destination, is real, and hop 4 or the link into it is the place to look; confirm with the host's own retransmit ratio and with a longer mtr run, since a 500-probe sample gives coarse resolution below a few tenths of a percent. A hop showing 100 percent with the destination answering is a router configured not to emit ICMP time-exceeded at all, which is common and means nothing.
L4.explanation: One rule covers all three cases: only loss that persists to the final hop is loss. Everything else is the control plane of an intermediate router telling you about itself.

L0.body:
The variables that turn a silent training hang into a readable one:

  NCCL_DEBUG=INFO                  print init, topology and algorithm choices
  NCCL_DEBUG=WARN                  only problems (a sane production default)
  NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,GRAPH,NET,TUNING,ENV     narrow the firehose
  NCCL_DEBUG_FILE=/logs/nccl.%h.%p.log            one file per host and pid

  NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=^lo,docker0   exclude interfaces; '=' is exact match
  NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5_0,mlx5_1        pin the RDMA devices per rank
  NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1                force TCP -- a DIAGNOSTIC, not a fix
  NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1               disable GPU peer access, to bisect
  NCCL_ALGO=Tree|Ring  NCCL_PROTO=LL|LL128|Simple   force a choice

  TORCH_NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1  hang -> timeout with a stack

  Rule: change ONE variable, re-run nccl-tests, compare busbw.
L0.cloze:
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO prints the discovered topology and the rings it chose; NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS narrows it to subsystems such as INIT, GRAPH, {{c1::NET}} and TUNING.
NCCL_DEBUG_FILE takes {{c2::%h}} and %p substitutions so ranks do not interleave into one stream.
Setting NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1 forces the {{c3::socket}} path and is a way to prove RDMA is the problem, never a fix.
NCCL_IB_HCA pins each rank to a named {{c4::HCA}}, which is how you correct a rank that picked a NIC across the socket boundary.
The method is to change {{c5::one}} variable at a time and re-measure with nccl-tests.

concepts.L1: NCCL's entire diagnostic surface is environment variables. They fall into three groups: ones that make it talk (DEBUG, DEBUG_SUBSYS, DEBUG_FILE), ones that constrain what it may use (SOCKET_IFNAME, IB_HCA, IB_DISABLE, P2P_DISABLE), and ones that force a choice it would otherwise tune (ALGO, PROTO, BUFFSIZE, NCHANNELS).
concepts.L2: The constraint variables get left in place after they fix a symptom. NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1 makes a hang go away by removing RDMA entirely, and the job then runs at socket bandwidth forever, with nobody able to explain the throughput because the cause is an environment variable in a launch script.
concepts.L3: Why the debug output is worth reading rather than grepping. NCCL_DEBUG=INFO answers the only question that matters at init: what does NCCL believe this machine is. It names the ring order per channel, the NIC per rank, the algorithm thresholds and the CPU affinity. Nearly every real performance fault is a disagreement between that belief and the hardware: a rank on a NIC across the inter-socket link, a NET/Socket fallback because /dev/infiniband was never mounted, or two channels where the topology supports twelve. Set NCCL_DEBUG_FILE with %h and %p so each rank writes its own file, then diff rank 0's against a rank you suspect. The difference is usually the bug, visible before a single step runs.

L4.prompt_tpl: Multi-node training runs but inter-node bandwidth is {frac} of expected. State the order in which you would set NCCL variables and what each would prove.
L4.answer: First NCCL_DEBUG=INFO with NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,GRAPH,NET and NCCL_DEBUG_FILE per host and pid, changing nothing else: this shows whether the transport is NET/IB or NET/Socket, which NIC each rank chose, and how many channels were built. A tenth of expected bandwidth is the signature of a socket fallback, so check that line first. Second, if IB is in use, compare each rank's chosen HCA against nvidia-smi topo -m and pin with NCCL_IB_HCA where a rank crossed the socket boundary; that explains a half or a third. Third, only after the topology reads correctly, run nccl-tests and look at the busbw curve against message size, then consider NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS or NCCL_BUFFSIZE, one at a time, re-measuring after each. Setting NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1 belongs in this sequence only as a control, to confirm what socket bandwidth actually looks like.
L4.explanation: The order matters: observe, then constrain, then tune. Tuning before reading the topology output means tuning a configuration you have not yet understood, and the knobs interact.

L4.prompt_tpl: A launch script contains {var} left over from an incident last quarter. State the effect on a healthy cluster today.
L4.answer: NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1 removes RDMA and routes every inter-node collective over TCP sockets, typically costing an order of magnitude of inter-node bandwidth while the job runs correctly and reports no error, so nobody connects the throughput to the variable. NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1 blocks direct GPU-to-GPU transfers, forcing intra-node traffic through host memory and destroying NVLink bandwidth, which shows up as tensor-parallel steps being far slower than the hardware allows. NCCL_ALGO=Ring forces the bandwidth-optimal algorithm onto every message size, so small collectives pay 2(n-1) serialised steps instead of 2*log2(n) and small-tensor-heavy workloads slow down badly. All three are diagnostics that were never removed. Grep the launch environment for NCCL_ before believing any performance number.
L4.explanation: Every constraint variable in this list makes a job correct and slow. Because none of them errors, the only defence is to treat a set NCCL_ variable as a finding in its own right.
